Many of us have been there: You book a flight through an airline's major hub, but your first segment is delayed and you miss your connecting flight, only to find out the next available flight with an open seat is hours away (or even the next morning). Or maybe you're trying to get home, but your flight is canceled, and you're stuck at your destination an extra night.

And when things go really wrong, it could be days before you can reach your destination.

There's no way to get that lost time back, but trip delay protection can come to the rescue if you used the right credit card to pay for your trip.

Trip delay protection reimburses reasonable out-of-pocket costs (lodging, meals, toiletries and local transportation) when a trip you paid for with an eligible card is delayed past a set threshold for a covered reason. You’ll pay these costs upfront, then file a claim for reimbursement so you're not left to cover those expenses yourself.

This coverage is secondary — meaning it only kicks in after you receive any other compensation. So if an airline provides food vouchers, you can't also request reimbursement for those meals. Even if the airline covers some expenses, you can still file a claim for any remaining expenses, like if you book a hotel at your own expense.

Importantly, a canceled flight is not automatically a covered trip delay. The cancellation generally must leave you stranded long enough to meet the policy's time requirement, result from a covered reason and involve a trip booked according to the card's payment rules.

Related: The best credit cards that offer trip cancellation and interruption insurance

While numerous travel rewards credit cards include trip delay protection, each policy is a little different.

*Eligibility and benefit level varies by card. Terms, conditions and limitations apply. Visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for details. Policies are underwritten by New Hampshire Insurance Company, an AIG Company.

Related: Can I get flight delay compensation? These are the ways you qualify

The $500 headline makes these policies look more alike than they are. In practice, they differ on how soon coverage begins, whether the cap scales with each traveler or ticket and whether the way you paid actually activates the benefit.

Being reimbursed per traveler means you actually have a much higher limit to work with. For example, if you're traveling as a family of four and spend a total of $800 on two hotel rooms, meals and transportation, you'd be reimbursed for all $800 if the policy is "per traveler", assuming everyone qualifies and all expenses are eligible. But if the card is capped at $500 per trip, you'll only get a $500 payout, regardless of how many people are traveling, leaving you to foot the rest of the bill.

For your travel to be covered, you must have paid for the original trip with the credit card that provides coverage. Some cards, like those issued by Capital One or Chase, include award travel if you paid for the taxes and fees on your flight with an eligible card.

However, other issuers, including American Express, require you to pay for the full cost of the trip with the card (or with reward points from the program). Amex also requires cardholders to pay for round-trip travel with their eligible card, though it's not as limiting as it sounds. Two separate one-ways still count, as long as both were purchased with the same card.

The also requires round-trip travel purchased on the card.

Before counting on coverage, read your card’s Guide to Benefits before you book.

Related: Times your credit card's travel insurance might not cover you

Trip delay coverage is only set up to cover expenses from lengthy delays rather than minor inconveniences. A minimum six-hour delay is required before coverage kicks in, and some cards require longer.

Some cards also allow for reimbursement of expenses during a forced overnight stay. That overnight provision makes some 12-hour policies more useful than they first appear because a flight that was supposed to take off at 10 p.m. and is now at 6 a.m. would qualify.

Every card in our table covers bad weather and equipment failure. Beyond that, the lists differ. Capital One and Chase also cover strikes. Amex and Citi don't, but they do cover lost or stolen passports.

Traffic or arriving late at the airport will not turn a missed flight into a covered delay. A previously announced or "known" disruption may also be excluded, so don't book a flight during a hurricane that's already started and expect to be covered.

Capital One has a pretty minimal umbrella of coverage when it comes to who's eligible. Trip delay protection usually only covers you, your spouse and your dependent children under the age of 22.

Chase has a more inclusive definition of family, including children (of any age), as well as parents, siblings, grandparents and more. Covered Chase family members also do not necessarily need to be traveling with the cardholder, as long as an eligible ticket was purchased with a qualifying card.

But Amex cards with this benefit generally cover companions who are traveling with you, even if they're unrelated, as well as tickets you purchased with your card on behalf of your spouse/domestic partner or unmarried dependent children up to age 19 (or under age 26 if a full-time student at an accredited college or university) even when they aren't traveling with you.

Chase doesn't list a maximum number of claims anyone can file, but American Express restricts you to two claims per eligible card per 12-month period. That distinction matters for frequent travelers.

Two claims may sound sufficient, but a frequent traveler could use both during one rough round-trip. For someone who flies regularly, an unlimited annual claim cap can be a meaningful advantage.

Claims can take weeks to be processed and paid out, which can make other card benefits you have useful in the meantime. Airport lounge access might cover the cost of food and drinks while you're waiting out a delay rather than having to collect and submit restaurant receipts, for example.

The exception is the : If your Alaska Airlines flight booked directly with Alaska on the card is delayed two hours or more, or canceled within 24 hours of departure, the primary cardholder automatically gets a $50 credit. It expires in 48 hours, so use it during the delay.

Though it's a modest credit, it can help cover your meal or transportation in real time, no paperwork required (and doesn't preclude you from filing a trip delay claim for other expenses later).

Related: Who is covered by your credit card travel insurance?

The most convenient way to file a claim is online through your card issuer's benefits website. You'll find the link within your online account or benefits guide. You can also initiate a claim by calling the phone number on the back of your card.

Usually, you must initiate a claim within 30 to 60 days of the event. I recommend opening the claim as soon as possible, even if you don't have all the receipts and paperwork yet. You'll typically have an additional grace period to submit all documentation after the claim has been formally opened.

Expect to provide four types of documentation:

Take screenshots of delay notifications, canceled segments and rebooking options before they disappear from the airline's app. Most airlines allow you to request statements confirming the delay and its reason through online customer service.

Related: Flight delayed? 4 things to do to get trip delay reimbursement from your credit card

When deciding between earning slightly more rewards and activating stronger insurance, the insurance may be the better trade on an expensive, complicated or disruption-prone itinerary. You'll also want to double-check that your trip delay coverage rules match how you actually booked.

Before travel, save your card's current benefits guide, use the card in the required way and keep every receipt. You certainly hope to never use this benefit, but it can be extremely valuable if you do.

#6208. Delta Air Lines Abruptly Cancels 1-Hour Airbus A350 Route: See Map Now

US airlines regularly deploy widebody aircraft on domestic routes, especially between major hubs and airports with significant connecting traffic. According to scheduling data from aviation analytics provider Cirium, thousands of domestic widebody flights are scheduled between December and October next year. Delta Air Lines alone has scheduled more than 17,000 domestic widebody flights, including around 660 operated by the Airbus A350-900.

One of the shortest routes on which the airline had planned to deploy the aircraft was the roughly one-hour flight between Harry Reid International Airport (LAS) in Las Vegas and Los Angeles International Airport (LAX). However, in its latest weekend schedule update, the SkyTeam member removed the A350 from that sector.

Delta had scheduled the A350-900 on the Las Vegas-to-Los Angeles route on just three occasions in January 2027. It was originally assigned to DL39 on January 4 and 5, departing Las Vegas at 7:05 PM and arriving in Los Angeles at 8:22 PM. A third service, operating as DL8783, was scheduled for January 3 with the same departure and arrival times.

According to AeroLOPA, the Atlanta-based carrier has two configurations of its A350-900 aircraft. The first accommodates 306 passengers, with 32 business class seats, 48 premium economy seats and 226 economy seats. The second has 275 seats, comprising 40 in business class, 40 in premium economy and 195 in economy. Delta had planned to deploy the latter configuration.

The planned A350-900 deployment may have been linked to the Consumer Electronics Show (CES), an annual technology trade show taking place in Las Vegas from January 6 to 9. The event attracts visitors from around the world, and Delta is increasing service to the city to meet expected demand.

The airline has confirmed it will operate more than 120 flights per day during the peak of CES 2027, connecting Las Vegas with major business markets in the US and overseas. Its plans include additional domestic frequencies and new nonstop international services from Hong Kong International Airport (HKG) and Taipei International Airport (TPE), two major Asian technology markets. Both routes will be operated by A350 widebody aircraft.

1 (Jan. 9); the other is planned for January 10 but using the A330-300

1 (Possible aircraft positioning; Jan. 4)

1 (Possible aircraft positioning; Jan. 5)

Cirium scheduling data also shows several other A350-900 flights planned to and from Las Vegas around the event, including services to Seoul Incheon International Airport (ICN), Paris Charles de Gaulle Airport (CDG) and Shanghai Pudong International Airport (PVG). The airline has also scheduled individual flights to Minneapolis–Saint Paul International Airport (MSP) and Salt Lake City International Airport (SLC), which may be related to aircraft positioning for its CES operations.

Delta is expanding its Airbus A350 network with four new deployments, including Manila, Riyadh, and additional Atlanta services.

Delta is one of the largest operators of the A350-900. According to ch-aviation, the airline currently operates a fleet of 43 aircraft of the type and is awaiting deliveries for 16 more (along with 20 A350-1000s). For January 2027, it has scheduled nearly 800 departures from US airports, with Los Angeles and Hartsfield–Jackson Atlanta International Airport (ATL) accounting for much of this activity.

Los Angeles is scheduled to see around eight to nine daily A350-900 departures most days, and Atlanta will see between seven and nine departures. By route, Atlanta to Seoul Incheon is the busiest, with two daily flights using the aircraft. This is followed by the domestic service between Atlanta and Los Angeles, where Delta has scheduled up to two daily A350-900 flights.

#6207. Gabe Evans announces 2028 comeback bid from Boebert’s district

Rep. Gabe Evans, here arriving at the Capitol in July for a House Republican Conference meeting, lost his bid for a second term representing Colorado's 8th District. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call) (Bill Clark CQ Roll Call)

Colorado Rep. Gabe Evans, who lost reelection earlier this month, announced Monday a 2028 run from the neighboring district of fellow defeated Republican Rep. Lauren Boebert.

“Now more than ever, Colorado needs conservatives in Congress who will fight to keep our border secure, cut taxes for working families, keep boys from dominating girls' sports and locker rooms, protect our water, and make energy affordable,” Evans said in a statement.

His announcement comes less than two weeks after he lost his bid for a second term representing the battleground 8th District in the Denver area. While the race had been considered one of the most competitive in the country, Democratic former state Rep. Manny Rutinel secured victory by 15 points.

As part of House Democrats’ massive midterm gains, they flipped three seats in Colorado. Boebert narrowly lost her reelection bid in the 4th District to Democrat Eileen Laubacher, while Republican Rep. Jeff Crank lost in the 5th District.

Evans’ statement cited his ties to the 4th District, which encompasses the eastern part of the state and extends into the Denver metro area.

“From Loveland to Lamar, I’m ready to keep fighting in the 4th District, where I grew up, and where my family has lived since 1976,” he said.

The district has a deep history of voting Republican. Boebert won by 11 points in 2024 while Donald Trump carried the district by 18 points.

Evans is far from the first member of Congress to switch to a district seen as more favorable to his party. Boebert herself shifted from Colorado's more competitive 3rd District to run for the heavily conservative 4th in 2024.

The 4th District will likely be a top target for Republicans in 2028, and Evans’ campaign sought to portray him as a clear front-runner in what could become a crowded GOP primary.

“Gabe Evans will enter 2027 and the race for Colorado’s 4th Congressional District with $300,000 in campaign funds and name recognition that no first-time candidate in the district could match,” his campaign said in the statement. “Combined with his record as an Army aviator, police officer, rancher, and member of Congress, that gives him a head start in money, name recognition, and credibility before the field takes shape.”

A former state legislator and Denver-area police officer, Evans also served 12 years in the Army. He was first elected to the House in 2024, unseating Democrat Yadira Caraveo, and currently sits on the Energy and Commerce and Homeland Security committees.

Laubacher, a Navy veteran who will take office on Jan. 3, is the first Democrat elected to represent the 4th District since Betsy Markey won her lone term in 2008. In response to Evans’ announcement, Laubacher’s campaign said she would be “focused on making Washington deliver” for district residents.

“There’s real work to do: ending the war in Iran that Gabe Evans voted six times to continue, lowering the cost of groceries and fertilizer that his eight votes for the tariffs helped drive up, and protecting the rural hospitals across the 4th district he voted to gut,” Laubacher spokesperson Taylor Gillespie said in a statement.

#6206. Emirates Finally Revamping Dubai Lounges: Temporary New First Class Lounge Now Open

Emirates is known for being a world-class airline, though at this point, the carrier’s ground experience at Dubai International Airport (DXB) leaves a lot to be desired, especially for premium passengers.

While I don’t want to suggest that the carrier’s first class lounges and business class lounges are terrible, they’re far from cutting edge, and the design definitely feels extremely outdated. Earlier this year, I wrote a post asking if Emirates was going to revamp its lounges at the airport, or just wait until the theoretical move to Dubai World Central (DWC) around 2032.

Well, it seems that my concerns have now been addressed, as Emirates has announced plans to completely transform its lounge experience in Dubai. Over the summer we saw the airline start to roll out a new global lounge concept for outstation lounges, and that idea is now coming to Dubai as well.

As is the case for any airline, rolling out a new lounge concept at a hub airport isn’t easy, given that it requires spaces to be closed. So that’s why it’s worth noting that Emirates is taking an innovative approach to refreshing its lounges in Dubai:

Emirates is investing a total of 400 million AED ($109 million) in these lounge spaces. Interestingly, Emirates claims that “all flagship lounges” will be getting a redesign, though there’s zero mention of the lounges in Concourse A, which are the biggest lounges in the world (they span the entire concourse), and offer direct boarding to planes. So it’s not clear when those lounges will undergo updates.

Here’s how Emirates President Tim Clark describes this development:

“Our customers expect the very best from Emirates, whether while flying or spending time with us on the ground. We believe the airport experience should be every bit as exceptional as the journey itself, and that’s why we are transforming our lounges globally. This new First Class Lounge in Dubai is the first taste of what’s to come. And if these are the lengths we will go to for a temporary lounge… just imagine what you can expect from new Emirates Lounges going forward. Over the next two years, we’ll be unveiling a completely different lounge experience, with new concepts in dining, wellness, entertainment and personalised hospitality. We’re going well beyond a traditional refurbishment and creating extraordinary spaces.”

We’ve already seen how Emirates is overhauling its global lounge network, and I’d say the changes are pretty awesome. So what can we expect in Dubai? As you can see, Clark references how the temporary new first class lounge is just a small glimpse into what we can expect in the future. Below is a video showing the new concept, and I must say, it looks impressive!

Here’s how Emirates describes the lounge concept, broadly:

Featuring immersive culinary experiences to dedicated wellness facilities and innovative entertainment concepts, Emirates is redefining what customers can expect from their time at the airport. Building on Emirates’ renowned hospitality, customers can expect distinct spaces for dining, relaxation, work and socialising – complemented by intuitive technology, refined interiors and elevated personal service. Each lounge will bear the hallmarks of the iconic Emirates brand, with the interiors conveying luxury, comfort, exceptional hospitality and global appeal.

When it comes to the temporary new first class lounge, here are the details:

As much as people like to suggest that Gulf carriers just throw money down the drain when it comes to passenger experience, Emirates is actually a pretty disciplined and cost focused business, which is also clear based on the fact that the airline still has angled business class seats with seven seats per row. 😉

But when the airline does invest and upgrade its products, it has a pretty good sense of what customers like. Barista coffee, Dom Perignon, and a gym? Count me in (though maybe the amenities shouldn’t be enjoyed in that order). 😉 It does sound like there still won’t be dedicated bedrooms, which would be disappointing, but also wouldn’t surprise me, given the volume of rooms they’d need to serve guests.

Emirates is hugely investing in its lounge network in Dubai, something that’s long overdue, if you ask me. Over the next two years, at least four lounges will be getting a full makeover, to match the carrier’s new lounge aesthetic.

We’ve just seen the opening of a new temporarily first class lounge in Concourse B, which is described as an example of what’s to come. Next year that lounge is expected to become a business class lounge, as a new flagship first class lounge opens, along with additional first and business class lounges.

The new design aesthetic looks great, and it sounds like some thought is being put into amenities as well. I look forward to seeing this transformation, though I can’t help but wonder if this reflects a delay with Emirates moving to its new hub airport.

What do you make of Emirates’ new lounge concept?

What I love most is that I don't have to spend hours scrolling through my credit card accounts looking for offers to activate. CardPointers does the heavy lifting for me, automatically adding eligible offers and helping me take advantage of savings I might otherwise miss. There's nothing quite like getting a surprise statement credit for a purchase you were going to make anyway.

I've conservatively saved several hundred dollars this year alone, including credits on everything from fast food to luxury hotel stays. And it's not just about the money. The time I've saved and the peace of mind that I'm not leaving valuable credit card benefits on the table make the service even more worthwhile.

While the free version is a good place to start, I think the premium CardPointers+ membership is well worth the $100 annual price, particularly for anyone juggling multiple rewards credit cards. And with the current 50% off promotion, it's an even more compelling deal. In fact, I like the service so much that I'm planning to upgrade to a lifetime membership.

If you're serious about maximizing your credit card rewards, benefits and statement credits, CardPointers is one of those tools that can quickly pay for itself. It's become an essential part of my credit card strategy, and I can't imagine managing my growing collection of cards without it.

#6204. Avelo Airlines Cancels Massive 31 Routes: See Full List Now

Avelo Airlines' network for the winter 2026/27 season looks rather different to how it did in 2025/26. Most notably, 31 of the routes the carrier served this time last year are not being operated this time around, with 25 domestic and six international. Of the domestic cuts, a third are concentrated at one airport, highlighting the brutally competitive nature of the airline industry in the States.

On the international side, scheduling data from Cirium, an aviation analytics company, shows that all of the cuts impact short-haul services to key leisure markets in Mexico and the Caribbean. While the last year has seen Avelo make various route cuts, the airline is in flux, and it has a lot to look forward to fleet-wise with the Embraer E2 set to modernize its ops. The airline has ordered 50, with deliveries from 2028.

Wilmington International Airport (ILM) in North Carolina is a common factor when examining Avelo's winter network versus 12 months ago. Overall, the facility has lost winter service to nine destinations, four of which are in Florida: Fort Lauderdale-Hollywood International Airport (FLL), Southwest Florida International Airport (RSW), Orlando International Airport (MCO), and West Palm Beach.

The remaining five route cuts concerned services from Wilmington to destinations in the northeast of the US. These included major hubs such as Detroit Metropolitan Wayne County Airport (DTW) and Washington Dulles International Airport (IAD), as well as smaller destinations such as Islip, Manchester, and Rochester.

Avelo commented on its presence in Wilmington in a statement obtained earlier this year by Wilmington Biz.

"Wilmington is also not a protected airport. Most of the affected routes cannot handle more than one airline serving them due to demand."

While Wilmington has been the hardest-hit airport by Avelo's winter cuts, it is far from the only US facility to have lost routes. Elsewhere in North Carolina, the carrier is no longer serving five destinations from Raleigh-Durham International (RDU) that it did this time last year: these are Albany, Fort Myers, Grand Rapids, Manchester, and Rochester. Of course, the cuts extend beyond North Carolina.

For instance, Tweed New Haven Airport (HVN) has lost three winter Avelo Airlines routes: William P. Hobby Airport (HOU), Louis Armstrong International Airport (MSY), and Washington Dulles International Airport (IAD). Wilmington in Delaware (ILG) saw three cuts, namely to Jacksonville (JAX), Nashville (BNA), and Raleigh-Durham, while Nashville itself lost Rochester.

Returning to the state of North Carolina, Concord-Padgett Regional Airport (USA) no longer handles winter Avelo Airlines flights to West Palm Beach. Elsewhere, the American ultra-low-cost carrier also no longer flies from Islip to Lakeland Linder International Airport (LAL) in Florida in the winter. Still, it remains relatively busy, with 1,616 flights scheduled to operate this November. These will offer 300,784 seats.

Avelo Airlines is about to get more tools for success.

On the international side, Wilmington International Airport has also lost winter Avelo Airlines flights to Punta Cana International Airport (PUJ) in the Dominican Republic. The carrier has also ceased its winter services to this popular Caribbean leisure destination from Bradley International Airport (BDL) in Windsor Locks, Connecticut, and Raleigh-Durham International Airport (RDU).

Windsor Locks has also lost winter Avelo Airlines flights to Cancún International Airport (CUN) in Mexico, and the carrier has ceased winter service from both Windsor Locks and Raleigh-Durham to Sangster International Airport (MBJ) in Montego Bay, Jamaica. The cessation of these routes marked the end of Avelo Airlines' international flights, which had only commenced operations back in 2024.

#6203. FAA Technician Only Unlocked The Door: Inside The Oversight Gap Behind The Nationwide Ground Stop

Last Friday we saw the worst disruption to air travel that we’ve seen in the United States in over 25 years, as air traffic shut down nationwide for over four hours. We quickly learned that this happened because L3Harris, a government contractor, was doing maintenance to switch telecommunications lines from copper to fiber.

The logical question is how something going wrong with the work of one contractor could cause our entire aviation ecosystem to shut down:

So, what’s actually going on here? A new report sheds some more light on this…

CNN has some insights into how little oversight there was of the work being performed by FAA contractor L3Harris, which led to the ground stop disaster that we saw. When was oversight reduced? Well, in early 2025, coinciding with the FAA laying off a large number of employees, as part of Elon Musk’s “Department of Government Efficiency” (DOGE) stunt.

According to this report, last Friday morning, an FAA technician escorted a contractor from L3Harris into a remote radio communications site for air traffic control in southern Arkansas, to replace a decades-old router. The FAA technician’s belief was that his role was done once the contractor entered the facility, according to people familiar with what happened, plus the union representing FAA employees.

That router replacement ended up being what triggered the communications issues across the country, ultimately leading to the nationwide ground stop.

FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford insists that the L3Harris engineer performing the upgrade “was monitored by an FAA technician” and that a risk assessment was performed, but sources dispute that characterization, pointing out that the technician “was only there to unlock the door,” and that “there was no monitoring.”

Funny enough, an FAA spokesperson later contradicted Bedford, saying “the FAA escort is responsible for providing the L3Harris technician access to and from the building,” and “because it is L3 equipment, the escort is not there while the technician is doing work.” It’s amazing how they can’t even keep their narrative straight.

This type of hands-off arrangement is apparently a recent development that happened under the Trump administration, and a change to how the FAA used to handle things. In March 2025, an FAA memo laid out changes to how FAA maintenance and upgrades would be carried out, in order to speed things up. The memo stated that “it is critical to approve maintenance performed by the Telecommunication Vendors without delay.”

With this policy, the FAA also went from receiving maintenance “requests” from private contractors that needed to be approved, to receiving “notifications” of intended work, noting that “this work will proceed without FAA approval,” if not processed in time.

While the memo claimed that an FAA liaison will evaluate the “purpose, severity, criticality and impact” of the work, there are reportedly only a handful of liaisons nationwide, processing thousands of notifications. In this case, L3Harris reportedly submitted its “notification” with just a few days notice, meaning there was no meaningful oversight.

A spokesperson for the union representing FAA employees explains that “orders were to simply let the contractor in the building,” that he “had no direction to help or assist in any way,” and that “no PASS-represented employee was asked to conduct a risk assessment on this particular upgrade.”

DUFFY: How many times does this have to happen before congress gives the money to fix it?R: You’ve been in office almost two years now, Republicans controlled both chambers of congress and still do.DUFFY: What your network are you from? pic.twitter.com/xuX5arTwjl

It also has to be pointed out that the March 2025 memo about a reduction in oversight came just weeks after Elon Musk’s DOGE laid off hundreds of FAA employees, making for the biggest single year layoffs at the organization in history.

That’s the beauty of slashing government inefficiency, right? If everything is working well, then we must not need all of those employees, eh? So to have a handful of people being “notified” of work and having to do an analysis sounds like it could be a problem.

We have to be honest, in general, politicians are really bad at accountability, and being honest when things go wrong. But whether you like Trump’s policies or not, there’s no denying that he takes lack of accountability to new levels. Everything good that happens is immediately his doing, and everything bad is Biden’s fault.

It would be nice if one Trump administration official actually had the introspection to say “hey, let’s make sure this doesn’t happen again,” rather than just yelling “give me $50 billion” and “Biden, Buttigieg, Biden, Buttigieg.”

We’re getting a clearer picture of the circumstances that caused the nationwide ground stop last Friday, the biggest disruption to US air travel since 9/11. A contractor with L3Harris was given access to a site to replace wiring, with virtually no oversight from an FAA employee.

While the FAA claims that there’s supposed to be oversight of contractor work, in this case the FAA employee was reportedly just tasked with unlocking the door. The approach to overseeing contractor work is reportedly a new system as of March 2025, where contractor work went from being viewed as “requests” to being viewed as “notifications,” with just a handful of people to oversee these requests. This came just weeks after hundreds of employees were laid off from the FAA, thanks to Musk’s DOGE.

What do you make of this FAA contractor oversight situation?

If any one piece of equipment let alone one in a remote corner of a network can bring down the whole things that's an unimaginably poor design.

#6202. White House budget aide Ueland slated to head GAO

Eric Ueland, No. 2 official at the White House Office of Management and Budget, arrives for his confirmation hearing in the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee on April 3, 2025. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

President Donald Trump on Monday nominated Eric Ueland, deputy director for management in the White House budget office, to be the next comptroller general to lead the Government Accountability Office.

The nomination fills in the blanks after Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Chairman Rand Paul, R-Ky., had scheduled a Nov. 19 hearing to examine more than a dozen of Trump’s nominees for executive and judicial positions but without identifying who the comptroller general candidate would be. Ueland's name has since been added to the hearing agenda.

The move sets up an unprecedented scenario where a top official of the Office of Management and Budget, a White House office that has tangled with the Government Accountability Office since Trump’s first term, is put forward as the next head of the legislative agency.

The GAO, a congressional watchdog with some 3,000 employees, has repeatedly accused the administration of violating the 1974 budget law by withholding or "impounding" enacted, appropriated funds. In September, for example, the GAO said Trump’s cancellation of $810 million in spending without the approval of Congress through a so-called pocket rescission was illegal.

White House Budget Director Russ Vought was quick to respond on X, writing that GAO “has become hyper partisan and ... they make their legal assessments based on whether Democrats are in the White House.” The administration has dismissed GAO opinions, arguing the agency has no authority over the executive branch because it is part of the legislative branch.

Democrats immediately denounced Ueland's nomination, saying it promised to further inflame tensions between the executive and legislative branches over the power of the purse.

“It would be lunacy for the Senate to hand a 15-year term leading Congress’ nonpartisan watchdog to a Russ Vought acolyte who spends his days plotting new ways for this administration to defy Congress," said Senate Appropriations ranking member Patty Murray, D-Wash., who is likely to chair the panel next year.

"Ueland orchestrated the president’s destructive mass firing campaign, is presiding over the razing of USAID, and is the last person who should be leading GAO," Murray said in a statement.

Sen. Gary Peters, D-Mich., ranking member of the Homeland Security committee, urged all senators to oppose the Ueland nomination, saying it would provide “further power to the Executive Branch at a time when independent oversight from Congress is needed more than ever.”

Peters also reiterated his previous criticism of Republicans for skipping bipartisan deliberations by a special 10-member legislative commission that is charged under statute with recommending candidates to the president for nomination.

“All three times the Commission process has occurred in the past, the president has selected a nominee with bipartisan support,” Peters said.

In a sign of potential trouble for the nomination, a few Republicans expressed qualms about Ueland and what critics described as a rushed process for picking a GAO chief.

"I'm not a fan," said retiring Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., who faulted Ueland's boss for not providing proof of the cost savings claimed by Trump's Department of Government Efficiency, known as DOGE.

"To me, there's a lack of discipline or business experience in there to answer that simple question, or the reason they don't answer it is they don't have an answer," Tillis said. "Both are bad."

While Tillis stopped short of promising to oppose Ueland, he said the nomination "deserves individual consideration" instead of being taken up in a group with several other nominees.

And Sen. John Curtis, R-Utah, "has concerns that the nomination is too partisan, particularly given how independent and long-term the appointment of the Comptroller General is," a spokesman said in a statement.

Ueland has served as deputy director for management at the White House budget office since last year following his confirmation by the Senate on a party line 52-45 vote. He also has been performing the duties of the OMB controller since September 2025, according to his LinkedIn profile.

An expert on legislative procedure and strategy, Ueland has worked in a wide range of administrative and policy-oriented positions in the executive branch — including at OMB, the State Department and White House — and before that in the Senate.

He served as director of legislative affairs for Trump in his first term, as well as the State Department undersecretary for civilian security, democracy and human rights, and director of the department’s Office of U.S. Foreign Assistance, among other positions.

Before that, he was the Senate Budget Committee’s GOP staff director under then-Chairman Michael B. Enzi, R-Wyo., for four years through the end of 2017.

Earlier, he worked as chief of staff to then-Senate GOP Whip Don Nickles of Oklahoma and then-Senate Majority Leader Bill Frist of Tennessee.

Ueland, who has a bachelor’s degree in history from the University of San Francisco, lacks the financial background of recent past comptrollers. He has, however, gone deep in the weeds with numbers at OMB and the Senate Budget Committee, and has extensive experience as an administrator.

Former comptroller Charles A. Bowsher was a CPA, a partner at Arthur Anderson and assistant secretary of the Navy for financial management before President Ronald Reagan tapped him to lead the GAO in 1981.

David M. Walker, his successor, was a CPA, a partner at Arthur Anderson, assistant secretary of labor in the Employee Benefits Security Administration, and deputy executive director of the Pension Benefit Guaranty Corporation before his nomination by President Bill Clinton.

Gene L. Dodaro, whose 15-year term ended last year, had a bachelor’s degree in accounting and had worked at GAO for some 35 years before President Barack Obama nominated him to succeed Walker.

When Dodaro left, he designated Orice Williams Brown, who was GAO’s chief operating officer, as acting comptroller.

Before Trump nominated Ueland, the six Republican members of the legislative commission sent a letter to the White House last week recommending three candidates for the position — Ueland, Brian C. DeBusk and Roland Foster, according to sources.

DeBusk is president and CEO of DeRoyal Industries, a privately held medical equipment manufacturer. He served on the Medicare Payment Advisory Commission from 2016 to 2022 after being appointed by Dodaro. Foster is a longtime GOP aide currently serving as senior adviser to retiring Sen. Joni Ernst, R-Iowa.

#6201. Atmos Rewards Business Card Changes: Higher(ish) Fee, New Benefits

Atmos Rewards is the loyalty program of Alaska and Hawaiian, and that includes three co-branded credit cards. There’s only one business credit card in the portfolio, and that’s the Atmos™ Rewards Visa Signature® Business Card.

Along those lines, there’s a major update, as the card has just undergone a full refresh. The bad news is that the card’s annual fee has gone up considerably (at least for most people), and the benefits have also changed. Let’s take a look, because as you’d expect, the changes are a mixed bag.

The good news is that there’s a huge incentive to apply for the card, given the massive limited-time welcome bonus of 90,000 Atmos Rewards points after spending $6,000 within the first 90 days.

Link: Learn more about the Atmos™ Rewards Visa Signature® Business Card

The Atmos Rewards Business Card is undergoing some major updates. This includes a higher annual fee, new rewards structure, and new set of perks. However, these changes only apply to new card members, as existing card members will keep the old benefits (and fee).

Let me emphasize that the card has a huge limited time welcome bonus of 90,000 Atmos Rewards points after spending $6,000 within the first 90 days. So that’s a major incentive to apply for the card, if you’re eligible. I value Atmos Rewards points at 1.5 cents each, so to me, that’s worth $1,350.

With that out of the way, let’s go over the details…

The Atmos Rewards Business Card now has a flat $195 annual fee, which covers the primary card member and any employee cards. Previously, the card had an annual fee of $70 per company, plus $25 per employee, so the minimum annual fee you’d pay would be $95.

It goes without saying that this change represents a significant increase in the annual fee, unless you had more than four employee credit cards on your account.

The Atmos Rewards Business Card also has a new rewards structure. The card now offers:

What has changed here is the new 10x points for booking through Atmos for Business (great for those who can use it), as well as a full overhaul of the 2x points categories. Previously the card offered 2x points on eligible gas, EV charging stations, shipping, and local transit purchases (including rideshare), while now it just offers 2x points on dining. As before, the card offers one status point for every $3 spent, with no cap.

The Atmos Rewards Business Card is picking up quite a few new benefits that it didn’t previously offer:

The refreshed card also keeps a first checked bag free and preferred boarding on Alaska and Hawaiian flights for the card member and up to six guests on the same reservation when the trip is paid with the card, a 20% rebate on eligible inflight purchases, a 10% rewards bonus for cardholders with an eligible Bank of America small business account, and no foreign transaction fees.

Let me emphasize that the card will no longer offer a $99 companion fare, so that’s being replaced by the new 50% off vouchers that can be earned with spending.

As of November 18, 2026, customers who apply for a new Atmos Rewards Business Card will be receiving the refreshed card, with the new benefits and fee.

Applications submitted before November 18 will continue under the prior card offering. What’s interesting is that current cardholders will keep their existing benefits, and will not be automatically moved over. However, you can call up Bank of America if you’d like to see about the opportunity of switching.

As of now, it sounds like there are no plans to transition people to the new system, so existing card members shouldn’t be negatively impacted by this.

The Atmos Rewards Business Card changes are a mixed bag. First, I want to once again emphasize that since existing card members aren’t impacted by these changes, I don’t think there should be too much frustration here.

In the past, the Atmos Rewards Business Card basically felt like the business version of the $95 annual fee Atmos™ Rewards Ascent Visa Signature® credit card (learn more), while now the card feels more like a hybrid between that and the $395 annual fee Atmos™ Rewards Summit Visa Infinite® Credit Card (learn more), in terms of both cost and benefits.

Admittedly it’s hard to do an apples-to-apples comparison between personal and business cards, because at least in theory, they’re supposed to serve different purposes. So here’s my take:

So I don’t have a terribly strong take here, other than wishing that spending on the card were a bit more lucrative, and more competitive with what’s offered by the Atmos Rewards Summit Card. The Summit Card will continue to be my go-to card for Atmos Rewards.

The Atmos Rewards Business Card has just undergone some major changes, though they don’t impact existing card members. For new applicants, the card now has a $195 annual fee, compared to the old fee of $70 for the company, and $25 per person.

The card is also getting a new set of benefits, including a new rewards structure, additional perks, and new incentives for spending. People will have varying takes as to whether these changes are positive or negative, depending on their consumer patterns.

My biggest takeaway is that the bonus of 90,000 Atmos Rewards points upon completing minimum spending is excellent, and a great incentive to apply for the card.

What do you make of these Atmos Rewards Business Card changes?

The Capital One VentureOne Rewards is a no-annual-fee travel rewards card that earns Capital One miles.

The biggest draw here is the ability to earn transferable miles without paying an annual fee. You can get more value from your rewards by transferring miles to airline and hotel partners, or redeem them at a fixed rate toward travel purchases if you'd rather keep things simple.

The card doesn't charge foreign transaction fees and comes with a few travel perks, including complimentary Hertz Gold+ Rewards Five Star status.*

That said, the VentureOne's everyday earning rate is on the lower side. I'd recommend it primarily to travelers who want access to Capital One's transfer partners without paying an annual fee, rather than those looking to earn the most rewards on everyday spending.

*Upon enrollment, accessible through the Capital One website or mobile app, eligible cardholders will remain at that status level through the duration of the offer. Please note, enrolling through the normal Hertz Gold Plus Rewards enrollment process (e.g. at Hertz.com) will not automatically detect a cardholder as being eligible for the program and cardholders will not be automatically upgraded to the applicable status tier. Additional terms apply.

Related: How to choose the best credit card for you

The VentureOne doesn't offer the extensive travel benefits of its higher-tier counterparts, but it still has a handful of perks worth knowing about.

One of the VentureOne's most useful benefits is that it doesn't charge foreign transaction fees.

Some credit cards charge around 3% on purchases made abroad, which can add up over the course of an international trip.

With the VentureOne, you can make international purchases without worrying about additional card fees.

Related: Best credit cards with no foreign transaction fees

VentureOne cardholders can enroll in complimentary Hertz Gold+ Rewards Five Star status.

Normally, earning this status requires completing three rentals or spending $1,000 on eligible rentals in a calendar year.

This status can provide benefits such as vehicle upgrades when available and additional rewards on eligible rentals.

While I wouldn't recommend choosing the VentureOne solely for this perk, it's a nice addition for travelers who occasionally rent cars.

The VentureOne also includes several protections that may come in handy when traveling or making purchases.

These include auto rental insurance, extended warranty protection and travel and emergency assistance.

For coverage details, including terms and exclusions, refer to your card's guide to benefits. These aren't necessarily benefits you'll use regularly, but they can provide some reassurance.

Related: The best credit cards for purchase protection

One of the VentureOne's biggest advantages is that it earns flexible Capital One miles rather than rewards tied to a single airline or hotel program.

That gives you several ways to use your rewards, depending on how much effort you want to put into maximizing them.

The VentureOne earns 5 miles per dollar spent on hotels, vacation rentals and rental cars booked through Capital One Travel and 1.25 miles per dollar spent on everyday purchases.

To put that into perspective, spending $1,000 on everyday purchases would earn you 1,250 miles. Based on TPG's November 2026 valuation of 1.85 cents per Capital One mile, those miles would be worth approximately $23 when maximized through transfer partners.

That's not a particularly strong return, especially when other no-annual-fee cards offer higher earning rates.

Still, the VentureOne keeps things simple. You don't have to keep track of rotating bonus categories, and you'll earn miles on every purchase.

If you're more concerned with earning transferable miles without paying an annual fee than maximizing every dollar you spend, that might be enough for you.

One of the easiest ways to use your Capital One miles is to use them to pay for eligible purchases as a statement credit.

You'll get a fixed value of 1 cent per mile, meaning 20,000 miles would cover a $200 travel purchase. This can be especially useful for expenses that aren't always easy to book with traditional airline or hotel points, such as Airbnb stays or Uber rides.

I like this option for beginners because there's no need to search for award availability or figure out how different loyalty programs work. You can just make an eligible travel purchase with your card and use your miles to cover it afterward.

You can also redeem your miles for Amazon purchases, Capital One entertainment purchases, cash back and gift cards. However, these options generally offer less value than travel redemptions, so I'd stick with using miles for travel whenever possible.

Related: How to get the maximum value when redeeming Capital One miles

If you're willing to put in a little more effort, transferring your Capital One miles to airline and hotel partners can be a great way to get more value from your rewards.

Capital One has more than 15 transfer partners, including programs like Avianca LifeMiles, British Airways Club and Choice Privileges. Most transfers are at a 1:1 ratio, although some partners have different ratios.

Personally, I love transferring Capital One miles to airline partners like Virgin Atlantic Flying Club and Air France-KLM Flying Blue.

For example, I recently transferred 6,400 Capital One miles to Flying Blue to book a Scandinavian Airlines flight from Stockholm Arlanda Airport (ARN) to Amsterdam Airport Schiphol (AMS). I paid just $10.70 in taxes and fees for a flight that would have otherwise cost $163.95.

That worked out to about 2.39 cents per mile, well above TPG's valuation of Capital One miles. And while I booked through Flying Blue, I actually flew on Scandinavian Airlines (SAS) — a good example of how you can use one airline's miles to book flights on its partners.

Of course, not every transfer will give you that kind of value. I always recommend comparing the cash price of a flight to the number of miles you'd need to transfer.

I'd also avoid transferring miles before you have a specific redemption in mind, since transfers generally can't be reversed. Instead, find the flight you want, confirm award availability and then transfer your miles.

If you're new to points and miles, redeeming miles to cover travel purchases might be an easier place to start. But once you're comfortable with the basics, learning how to use transfer partners can really help you stretch your rewards further.

Related: How to transfer Capital One miles to airline and hotel partners

The VentureOne's biggest drawback is its relatively low everyday earning rate.

Earning 1.25 miles per dollar may be simple, but several competing cards offer higher returns without charging an annual fee — more on that below.

The VentureOne also lacks many of the travel benefits that make premium rewards cards appealing, including airport lounge access and annual travel credits.

If you travel frequently or put a significant amount of spending on your credit cards, you may find that paying an annual fee for a more rewarding card makes sense.

Related: How to decide if a credit card’s annual fee is worth paying

If you're considering the VentureOne, I'd also take a look at the Capital One Venture Rewards Credit Card.

Both cards earn transferable Capital One miles, but the Venture Rewards earns at least 2 miles per dollar spent on purchases, compared to the VentureOne's 1.25 miles per dollar spent. It also comes with a few additional travel perks, including up to a $120 statement credit every four years for the application fee for either Global Entry or TSA PreCheck

The trade-off is that the Venture Rewards has a $95 annual fee, while the VentureOne doesn't charge one.

Still, depending on how much you spend, that $95 could be worth paying. Based on TPG's valuation of 1.85 cents per Capital One mile, you'd need to spend about $6,850 a year on purchases earning the base rate for the extra miles to offset the Venture Rewards card's annual fee.

That's before factoring in welcome offers or other benefits. And if you typically redeem miles for travel statement credits at 1 cent apiece, you'd need to spend more to make up the difference.

Personally, I'd lean toward the Venture Rewards if you plan to use your card regularly and want to earn miles faster. But if avoiding an annual fee is your priority, the VentureOne still gives you access to the same transfer partners.

Related: Capital One Venture vs. VentureOne: Which card is right for you?

I think the VentureOne is worth considering if your priority is earning transferable travel rewards without paying an annual fee.

However, if you spend heavily on your card or travel frequently, the Venture Rewards or another higher-earning card could provide better long-term value.

There are currently two welcome offers available on the VentureOne, each with a different spending requirement:

Based on TPG's valuations, which peg Capital One miles at 1.85 cents apiece, these bonuses are worth $370 and $740, respectively.

The biggest difference between the two offers, aside from the bonus miles and spending requirements, is that the standard VentureOne offers a 0% introductory APR for 15 months on purchases and balance transfers, followed by a variable APR of 18.74%-28.74% (a balance transfer fee applies). The Miles Boost version doesn't offer this benefit.

Compared to the card's offer history, the standard 20,000-mile bonus has been available for most of the past few years, although Capital One briefly added a $100 travel credit to the offer in 2025.

The Miles Boost offer, on the other hand, matches the highest bonus we've seen on the VentureOne. So if you've been considering this card, now could be a particularly good time to apply for that version.

Personally, I'd lean toward the Miles Boost offer if you can comfortably meet the higher spending requirement and don't need the introductory APR benefit. You'll earn twice as many bonus miles for an additional $500 in spending.

Keep in mind that Capital One has a 48-month welcome bonus restriction across its Venture card family. If you've received a new cardmember bonus on the VentureOne, Capital One Venture Rewards Credit Card or Capital One Venture X Rewards Credit Card within the past 48 months, you won't be eligible for another VentureOne bonus.

However, earning a VentureOne bonus doesn't, on its own, prevent you from qualifying for a future Venture Rewards or Venture X welcome bonus.

Related: Evaluating the current offer on the Capital One VentureOne

The VentureOne isn't the only option for travelers who want to earn rewards without paying a high annual fee. Depending on your spending habits and travel goals, one of these cards could be a better fit.

For additional options, check out our full list of the best no-annual-fee cards.

The Capital One VentureOne offers something you won't find on every no-annual-fee card: the ability to earn miles that transfer directly to airline and hotel partners.

That makes it a reasonable starting point for travelers who want to explore transferable rewards without committing to an annual fee.

However, its modest earning rate makes it harder to recommend to anyone looking to maximize rewards on everyday spending.

If you're comfortable paying a modest annual fee, I'd consider the Venture Rewards instead. But if avoiding an annual fee is your top priority and you want access to Capital One's transfer partners, the VentureOne is worth a look.

#6199. The Airlines Set To Replace Their Boeing 777s With New 777-9s Throughout The 2030s

Boeing has roughly 620 orders for an aircraft that has not delivered a single one yet, and some of the very first examples built may never reach the airline that paid for them. The 777-9 is meant to be the jet that carries the world's biggest long-haul airlines through the 2030s, but the program is about seven years behind its original 2020 service date, and the biggest customer has already turned away its first batch. For an industry that plans fleets decades ahead, that is a very awkward way to start a new era.

So who is really lining up to replace their Boeing 777s with the new 777-9, what exactly are they replacing, and when will passengers see the first one? The answers involve Emirates, Qatar Airways, Cathay Pacific, Singapore Airlines, and Lufthansa, plus a rival Airbus that has already started delivering.

The scale of the commitment is hard to ignore. According to an order book compiled by Airways Magazine at the end of May 2026, the 777X program stood at 619 orders: 521 777-9s, 63 777-8 freighters, and 35 passenger 777-8s, all of them for Emirates. That is a remarkable number for an aircraft that has not carried a single paying passenger, and it makes the 777X Boeing's most important widebody bet of the decade. Airways also noted that the problem is certification, not demand, which is a rare thing to say about a program this delayed.

Emirates dominates the list. As reported by Emirates itself, its November 2025 Dubai Airshow deal added 65 more 777-9s, worth $38 billion at list prices, and lifted its total to 270 777Xs. The airline also holds options to convert part of that order into the 777-8 or the proposed, larger 777-10. Airways lists the split as 235 777-9s and 35 777-8s, so the exact mix is still fluid. Qatar Airways is second with 124 aircraft, made up of 90 777-9s and 34 777-8 freighters, followed by Cathay Pacific with 35 and Singapore Airlines with 31.

British Airways and its parent IAG have 24, Lufthansa Group has 27 (20 passenger jets and seven freighters), Korean Air has 20, and ANA has 20, including two freighters. Air India, Etihad, and Ethiopian Airlines hold 10, 10, and 8. But a long list of customers only tells us who wants the jet. It says nothing about what each of them plans to retire in exchange, or how long they will have to keep the old aircraft flying while they wait.

For most buyers, the answer is the Boeing 777-300ER, the best-selling long-haul widebody of its generation. Emirates alone flies 119 of them, plus 10 777-200LRs, according to its own fleet table. As noted by Simple Flying, the 777X is also pitched as a successor to high-capacity four-engine jets such as the Boeing 747 and the Airbus A380, which burn far more fuel and cost more to maintain.

The new jet's biggest selling point is efficiency. According to Simple Flying's analysis of range and capacity, the 777-9 seats around 426 passengers against roughly 396 on a 777-300ER, while keeping a nearly identical range. The GE9X engines are expected to deliver up to 10% better fuel efficiency than the GE90-115B engines on the older jet.

The wing is the other trick: it spans 235 feet, 5 inches (71.8 meters) in flight, but its tips fold to 212 feet, 9 inches (64.9 meters) on the ground so it still fits standard gates. Boeing's pitch to airlines is simple: keep the long range, burn less fuel, and spend less on maintenance than the aging jets on the ramp.

Boeing 777-300ER vs. 777-9: the swap in numbers

On paper, that is a clean trade: more seats, similar range, lower fuel burn. The uncomfortable detail is that the older jets have to keep flying while the replacement is late, and that raises a very practical question about timing. Airways Magazine points out that carriers waiting on the 777-9 have had to stretch the lives of older 777-300ERs, A380s, and 747-400s, which adds maintenance, fuel, and cabin-product pressure with every extra year.

Boeing has never revealed what a pair of 777X wings costs. The clues point to a surprisingly large number.

Lufthansa will be the first, with Boeing targeting a 2027 delivery. Emirates said in November 2025 that it expects its first 777-9 from the second quarter of 2027, and its Boeing deliveries stretch all the way to 2038. That means the airline will be swapping 777-300ERs for 777-9s for more than a decade, which is exactly why this story belongs to the 2030s rather than to next year. Emirates still flies 116 Airbus A380s as well, so the transition will be gradual rather than a clean break.

Others will wait longer. According to Simple Flying, citing the Mainly Miles blog, Singapore Airlines' fleet plan shows no 777-9 deliveries in the 12 months to March 31, 2027, with Emirates, Qatar Airways, and Lufthansa ahead in the queue. That timing matters because Singapore Airlines is also planning a new premium economy product around the aircraft, making the 777-9 part of a future cabin strategy as well as a fleet replacement program.

Even the schedule itself is soft. Airways Magazine reported that FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford signaled the 777X would follow the 737 MAX 7 and MAX 10 into 2027 for certification. So queue position is one thing, but the airlines cannot simply take delivery because they are next in line. The more awkward problem is already sitting on Boeing's property: aircraft built years ago for customers that may no longer want them.

Between 2019 and 2021, Boeing built around 30 777-9s before the program stalled, including aircraft earmarked for Emirates and Lufthansa, according to German aviation outlet aero.de. By the time they could be delivered, they would be about eight years old and technically behind the final production standard. That creates an unusual problem for a brand-new aircraft: the earliest examples are already old enough to require substantial work before an airline wants them.

As reported by Simple Flying, Emirates rejected the first batch built for it because bringing those airframes up to the required standard would take extensive and costly rework. Boeing reportedly dismantled one early Emirates-bound 777-9 after the cost to fix it exceeded its value. Lufthansa has since said, on its second-quarter earnings call, that it will refuse some of its earliest aircraft, with Boeing contributing financially to upgrade the rest.

Qatar Airways has reportedly signaled that it does not want early-build aircraft either, so Boeing may pool the rejected jets and sell them in bundles. According to aero.de, an unnamed US airline is reportedly interested in 20 early 777-9s, which is striking because no major US carrier has ordered the type at all. A discounted early-build 777-9 could therefore find a new home, but the fact that airlines that ordered the aircraft in the first place are turning some away shows just how unusual this delay has become.

The aircraft is gaining ground as Boeing's 777X slips further behind schedule, reshaping the battle for long-haul dominance.

According to Simple Flying, Qatar Airways put the A350-1000 into service in February 2018, the 777-9 first flew in January 2020 and still was not certified at Farnborough 2026, and Airbus has already delivered 114 A350-1000s against 367 firm orders. Boeing, meanwhile, has delivered none of its more than 520 777-9s.

Air Canada is the clearest example. As reported by Business Traveller, the airline ordered eight A350-1000s, with options on eight more, for delivery from the second half of 2030, to modernize a long-haul fleet that includes 19 777-300ERs. Business Traveller calls the A350-1000 a logical replacement for the 777-300ER, and says it brings a cabin altitude of about 6,000 feet (1,829 meters) versus 8,000 feet (2,438 meters) on the 777 family. No North American airline has ordered the 777-9, so for passengers in the US and Canada, the A350-1000 may arrive first.

Still, a head start is not the same as a better fit. The 777-9 carries more passengers, and for airlines that fill every seat, that may be the decisive metric. The A350-1000 offers the established nine-abreast cabin and a substantial operating track record, while Boeing's aircraft offers greater capacity and is aimed squarely at airlines that need to move huge numbers of passengers through constrained hubs. That leaves the 777-9 with a clear market, but a narrower one than the raw order total might suggest.

The honest answer is volume and density. Emirates and Qatar Airways run some of the busiest trunk routes in the world, and for those carriers, the 777-9's size is a feature rather than a flaw. An A350-1000 cannot match its seat count, and the A380 is out of production, so the 777-9 is effectively the last big twin-engine option left for airlines that need capacity above all else. That is the strongest argument Boeing has, and it is also why the aircraft is best suited to a relatively small group of mega-hub operators.

The test comes in the next 18 months. If Lufthansa takes its first jet in 2027 and Emirates follows soon after, the long order book will start to look like a steady delivery stream. If certification slips again, as Airways Magazine warns could compress the entire handover and training timeline, more carriers may do what Air Canada did and look at the A350-1000 instead. The early-build jets will be worth watching too: how many Boeing can remarket, and at what price, will reveal just how costly the delay has been.

Emirates has even signed options to stretch part of its order into the 777-10, a bigger variant Boeing is still studying. That may ultimately be the most revealing sign of all: the airlines that have waited longest for the 777-9 are still thinking about what comes after it. By 2035, the question may no longer be whether the 777-9 replaced the 777-300ER. It may be whether Boeing's biggest twinjet has finally found the narrow but extremely valuable market it was designed for.

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

#6197. New aviation funding request hits Senate turbulence

Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., speaks with reporters on Nov. 10. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

Senate Republicans appeared skeptical Monday about the need for as much as $50 billion to upgrade the nation’s aging air traffic control system, after a nationwide ground stop last Friday prompted the massive, increased asking price from top administration officials.

Speaking with reporters, Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., said he believed the department still had about $8 billion outstanding from an air traffic control modernization package included in last year’s reconciliation law.

“I got to obviously see the explanation behind it, or sort of laying out the numbers why it's necessary,” Thune said of the $50 billion, which jumped from $30 billion a day earlier.

Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., told reporters he was unimpressed by Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy’s request and that he wanted to see a breakdown of how the department would use the funds.

“They got to give us an update,” Tillis said. “I mean, the $50 billion request — I thought that was $30 billion. So people have got to explain to me, really, even the basis for the $30 billion, let alone the additional $20 billion that Duffy mentioned the other day.”

Sen. John Hoeven, R-N.D., similarly said legislators would need “more detail” on the request but said “obviously there needs to be more” funding for the modernization efforts.

Hoeven serves on the Senate Transportation-HUD Appropriations Subcommittee, which rolled out a fiscal 2027 spending bill Monday that would increase the FAA’s annual allocation to facilities and equipment by $500 million, a nearly 13 percent boost.

Duffy is slotted to attend the Senate GOP conference lunch on Tuesday, where he is likely to be peppered with such requests for specifics. Meanwhile, FAA staff are expected to brief House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee aides on Tuesday, after that meeting got pushed on Monday.

The Senate’s go-slow approach is in contrast to Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., who said over the weekend that he would add the $50 billion request to a year-end legislative package.

The White House’s call for additional funds ballooned last week in the aftermath of the nationwide ground stop that created confusion and concern at airports around the country. The Federal Aviation Administration said Sunday that the unusual move was made “out of an abundance of caution” after legacy equipment became flooded with data during routine upgrades.

The FAA’s initial investigation tied the data flooding to work being done at a radar site in Texas and a radio communications site in Arkansas by contractor L3Harris Technologies.

Speaking on CNBC’s Squawk Box, Duffy said the server thought to have caused the flooding was taken to the L3Harris lab in Florida where FAA personnel are working with the FBI to analyze the router that likely caused the system instability.

Still, as administration officials attempt to understand the system errors that led to the ground stop, Duffy has used the moment as justification to lobby for additional funds.

“In this old telecom network, I do have money to switch over from the old copper wires to fiber and we’re 70 percent completed with that mission, but we need a brand new architecture for our telecom and aviation,” Duffy said on CNBC Monday. “This can happen quickly to build a new state of the art telecom network, it’s just that it has to be funded.”

A day before the incident, Duffy and Office of Management and Budget Director Russ Vought wrote to congressional appropriators, formally asking for $30.1 billion in added funds for the modernization effort, in line with a bill introduced by Sen. Eric Schmitt, R-Mo., in late September. That ask inexplicably jumped up to $50 billion by Friday night in the aftermath of the ground stop.

On Monday, Thune noted the prior request for approximately $30 billion, which he said included “some other stuff” as well.

Schmitt’s bill and the White House request would provide $10.1 billion for air traffic control upgrades, including $7.2 billion for a “common automation platform and a common controller workstation,” and $2 billion for cloud computing and telecommunications infrastructure.

Another $10 billion would go toward airport improvement projects, including $2 billion to “construct, replace, and improve terminal air traffic control facilities, including activities using digital tower technologies.”

The request includes $10 billion for a terminal modernization or reconstruction pilot program for certain midsized airports.

Thune said Monday that he tallied about $12 billion in the new request specifically for air traffic control related issues, likely a reference to the $10.1 billion plus the $2 billion for terminal facilities.

“I think there's more we need to figure out, and obviously I think we all agree that we need to be modernizing and updating, particularly in an area like that where safety is the number one priority, but also we want to do that in a smart way and make sure that we're using taxpayer dollars wisely and well,” Thune said. “We’ll hear him out.”

Meanwhile, Democrats kept up the drumbeat of criticism, both for the airspace management that led to the ground stop and the rollout of the new funding request.

“So typical of this incompetent administration — they have money, they don’t use it and then they come back and say ‘give us more money,'” Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., said on the floor.

Savannah Behrmann and Jacob Fulton contributed to this report.

#6196. Buy Air Canada Aeroplan Points With 100% Bonus (1.31 Cents Each): Worth It?

The Air Canada Aeroplan program is currently offering a bonus on purchased points. While this is a mystery bonus, where different members may be eligible for different offers, it seems the best version is for up to a 100% bonus.

Is there value with this offer? With a specific use in mind, absolutely, in my opinion. Aeroplan is one of my all-around favorite frequent flyer programs, thanks to the huge variety of airline partners, the ability to have stopovers on one-way awards for 5,000 points, and the generally great online booking experience.

Link: Buy Air Canada Aeroplan points with this promotion with up to a 100% bonus

Between 12AM PT on November 19 and 11:50PM PT on December 10, 2026, the Air Canada Aeroplan program is offering a promotion on purchased points.

Different members may be eligible for different offers, so you’ll want to log into your account to see what you’re eligible for. However, it appears that the best version of the offer is for up to a 100% bonus, structured as follows:

I should emphasize that other members seem to be eligible for offers of 85%, 90%, or 95%, so it’s no guarantee that everyone will see the 100% offer.

Ordinarily, Air Canada Aeroplan charges $0.0375 CAD (~0.026 USD) per point. Any purchases made with US credit cards and US billing addresses aren’t subject to sales tax either.

If you purchased 500,000 Aeroplan points with a 100% bonus, you’d receive a total of 1,000,000 Aeroplan points at a cost of $18,750 CAD (~$13,101 USD), which is a rate of 1.31 cents (USD) per Aeroplan point.

If you wanted to purchase the fewest possible points at the best possible price, you’d want to buy exactly 90,000 points at a cost of $3,375 CAD (~$2,358 USD), which would potentially get you 180,000 points, for the same cost per point.

While you can purchase up to one million Aeroplan points per account per calendar year, there’s ordinarily a per-transaction limit of 250,000 points pre-bonus. However, during this promotion that has been doubled, to 500,000 points.

Aeroplan points purchases typically post pretty close to instantly, though in some situations, it could take up to 72 hours for points to post. Note that the purchase of Aeroplan points is non-refundable, and Aeroplan points purchases also don’t count toward elite status.

When Air Canada Aeroplan offer a promotion on purchased points, we most commonly see a bonus in the range of 90-110%, but the exact offers do vary. Personally I’d buy points based on when you’re ready to redeem them, rather than the exact cost. After all, the cost to buy points with a 100% bonus vs. a 110% bonus isn’t vastly different.

Below is a chart with some of the recent promotions we saw from the Aeroplan program, before this one.

Air Canada Aeroplan points purchases are processed by points.com, meaning they don’t count as an airfare purchase for the purposes of credit card spending. Therefore I’d recommend using a card on which you’re trying to reach a minimum spending requirement, or otherwise, a credit card that maximizes your return on everyday spending.

Since the purchase of Aeroplan points is billed in CAD, there is one other great option. Beyond that, the best options would be cards that offer 2x transferable points, while having no foreign transaction fees.

Aeroplan is one of my favorite frequent flyer programs out there. To cover a few of the basics:

There are lots of phenomenal uses of Aeroplan points, and this is a program that I redeem through regularly. Just keep in mind that Aeroplan now has dynamic award pricing on select partners, including Emirates, Etihad, FlyDubai, and United, among others.

One of my favorite things about Air Canada Aeroplan is that the program has more airline partners than any other frequent flyer program, and you can redeem points on over 45 airlines. In addition to Air Canada belonging to the Star Alliance, Aeroplan also partners with airlines that include Etihad, Azul, Air Serbia, Virgin Australia, Air Dolomiti, Eurowings, Gulf Air, Oman Air, Air Mauritius, and Emirates.

Always look up award availability before buying points, to get a sense of what you can expect.

Everyone will value points currencies differently. Based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider Aeroplan points to be worth 1.4 cents each. However, I tend to value points pretty conservatively, and there are many ways to get way more value from Aeroplan points than that.

Air Canada Aeroplan points only expire after 18 months of inactivity. However, any account activity that leads to earning or redeeming points (including buying them) would reset the expiration.

While buying Aeroplan points could represent a great deal, keep in mind that there are lots of other ways to earn Aeroplan points. Most significantly, Aeroplan is transfer partners with American Express Membership Rewards, Bilt Rewards, Capital One, and Chase Ultimate Rewards, making the currency pretty easy to acquire. Air Canada’s Aeroplan program is offering a bonus on purchased points. While people may be targeted for different offers, it appears the best offer is for up to a 100% bonus, which kicks in as long as you purchase at least 90,000 points in one transaction. This is an opportunity to buy points for 1.31 cents (in USD) each.

This could represent a good deal, and there are plenty of situations under which the math will work out for this promotion. Still, in general I’d only recommend buying points with a short term use in mind, as there’s always risk to holding onto points for longer periods of time.
