#6176. Why Aerolíneas Argentinas Is Basically An Ultra Low Cost Carrier In Disguise

This might seem like a rather niche topic to cover in my first week at OMAAT, but after Ben mentioned this story in his intro article, I thought it made sense to follow up fast with an explainer.

As a flag carrier of the 3rd most populous nation in South America, I went into my Aerolíneas Argentinas flight with them at the start of the year expecting some pretty standard things: enjoying my SkyTeam benefits, lounge access, and, most importantly of all for someone living out of a suitcase, checked bag allowance.

However, I quickly discovered that the airline is basically an ultra-low-cost airline masquerading as a full-service carrier.

I needed to get from Buenos Aires to Mendoza for a friend’s 40th birthday celebrations. Options were pretty limited, with nonstop flights available with either JetSmart or, indeed, Aerolíneas Argentinas. I try to avoid low-cost airlines when possible, because, quite simply, I enjoy the flying experience, and low-cost airlines tend to suck every enjoyable element out of it.

Other pros to booking Aerolíneas Argentinas, personally:

After researching my options, I used Flying Blue miles to book two single tickets from Buenos Aires Jorge Newbery Aeroparque Airport (AEP) to Mendoza’s El Plumerillo Airport (MDZ).

I can’t remember how much the fares were when I was planning the trip, but each one-way flight cost a total of 7,500 miles and less than $10 in taxes and fees.

Looking now at example fares for January next year, round-trips for Aerolíneas’ lowest and most restrictive fare category (more on that to come) start at around $120.

I know it’s not a hard-and-fast rule, but I’ve come to expect that, most of the time, the baggage allowance listed on the booking confirmation is correct. This is often true with redemptions, such as British Airways, which notably offers and acknowledges a 23 kg baggage allowance when redeeming Avios, even for a short-haul flight in economy.

The confirmation email I received clearly noted 1x checked bag with a 23 kg limit.

Again, the attached PDF stated that I’d have 1x checked bag included.

As the Argentinian scamsters would have it, I learned at check-in that the airline has a 15 kg weight limit for checked bags on domestic flights. I tried to plead my case and showed the rather unhelpful check-in agent my booking confirmation, but he basically said, “that means nothing.”

So they weigh your bag, give you a ticket, and then you have to exit the terminal building and find this little cashier where they collect their scammy little earnings. And what better place to proudly display a “SkyTeam Alliance Member” sign at the very desk where the airline also proudly collects baggage fees from SkyTeam elite status holders, even when traveling on award tickets?

Once I’d been charged the fee of around $17, I had to join another queue back inside and show them I’d paid for the extra weight before they’d dispatch my bag. You might look at the $32 in fees I paid and think, “What is he complaining about?” But this isn’t about the actual amount of money; it’s the principle.

Only after the debacle did I learn the extent of Aerolíneas Argentinas’ domestic fare restrictions. Imagine paying $510 (more than four times the cheapest fare) for a “premium economy” ticket and still only getting 15 kg checked baggage allowance, no Fast Pass, no priority boarding (what?), and no lounge access. The latter isn’t such a big deal as Aerolíneas Argentinas doesn’t even have its own lounge at AEP.

Airline loyalty is really important to me, and I generally value it more than the ability to redeem miles. Maybe I’ll get into that another day…

Things got off to a fairly normal start when I saw the Sky Priority check-in kiosks at Aeroparque.

That feeling of normalcy lasted as long as it took me to get from the sign to the aforementioned conversation about the checked bag situation at the desk. Despite my very best efforts combining my Castilian Spanish and Geordie charm (we’re called Geordies where I’m from in the North East of England), the man at the check-in desk seemed to take real pleasure in explaining that the checked bag rules on my booking confirmation were irrelevant and I’d have to pay the fee.

For what it’s worth, Sky Priority check-in was also available at Mendoza.

Being nickel-and-dimed for a checked bag by a flag carrier airline is shameful.

Back at Aeroparque, there was no fast track, and the security line was ridiculously long. That said, it’s rare in South America to have fast track lanes. For example, no matter whether you’re flying economy or first class (even Air France La Première), everyone waits in the same line to clear pre-departure passport control at São Paulo’s Guarulhos.

Thanks to my Priority Pass, I did have access to the surprisingly nice AMAE lounge in the national departures part of the airport.

Even from the outside, my 15-year-old Embraer 190 looked like it had seen better days. The zebra-striped dirt streaks running from each window suggested this place hadn’t been washed or hit the maintenance hangar for a while.

Inside the Embraer, however, could have been a lot worse. The older seats had thick padding, and despite being a small 2-2-configured cabin, it felt bright and spacious.

It was the Uber advertising on every single headrest that I found most jarring.

The legroom was decent, too. The retro seatback screens, on the other hand, were pretty much redundant.

It was stepping on board the 16-year-old Boeing 737-700 back to Buenos Aires that Aerolíneas Argentinas’ low-costness was most glaring. Looking at this, I would never guess this plane belonged to a flag carrier. The seats were very uncomfortable, and I think I remember they didn’t recline either.

As for service, I don’t recall it being particularly good or particularly bad. Forgettable is probably the most accurate word.

Imagine the likes of Spirit (RIP) or Ryanair calling itself a national flag carrier; that’s basically what Aerolíneas Argentinas is. I’m planning a trip with my dad and brother for February next year that includes Argentina, and I will actively avoid flying Aerolíneas, even if it means forgoing the chance to earn any Flying Blue miles and XPs.

It’s almost as if the airline has been abandoned. After all, the only real competition is low-cost airlines at LATAM — the full-service carrier which dominates South America. Who knows, maybe things will change come 2028 when it takes delivery of new Airbus A330-900s and Boeing 737 MAXs.

If I were a power that be at SkyTeam, I’d definitely remove the airline from the alliance. And if I had my way, Aerolíneas Argentinas would be bought by LATAM, and the cherry on top would be LATAM joining SkyTeam. I should probably put a business case together for that…

#6174. End Of An Era: American Retires Boeing 777 Flagship First Class

American Airlines has just officially “retired” its Flagship First product on the Boeing 777-300ER, meaning that no US carrier offers an international first class product anymore. The good news is that an updated business class product is in the process of being rolled out, and that’s something that should benefit a lot of travelers.

As I’ve covered in the past, American is in the process of eliminating its “premium” first class product, and that change was just implemented for flights as of this week on the carrier’s biggest planes.

Specifically, the Boeing 777-300ER is American’s “flagship” aircraft, with 20 of the planes in the fleet. As of this week, the airline is no longer selling first class on these planes. Now, plenty of 777-300ERs with these cabins are still flying around, as American has just started reconfiguring its 777-300ERs with new cabins, including the new business class.

Still, for flights effective immediately, first class seats are just being sold as standard business class seats, and any business class passenger can select seats in the first two rows (you’d think they’d try to charge extra or at least reserve them for select elite members, but nope). So there will no longer be a differentiated soft product… not that there was much of a difference as of late anyway!

I expect we’ll continue to see these planes flying around well into late 2027, or possibly even into 2028, depending on how fast the retrofit project happens. American’s dedicated first class ground product has also largely been discontinued, as Flagship First Dining has turned into Flagship Dining, so a la carte lounge dining is now available to eligible business class passengers as well.

It’s great that these planes will be getting new business class suites, as they’ll also be the aircraft belonging to a US carrier with the most business class seats, as they’ll have 70 of them… that’s lot!

While American has now eliminated its international first class product, it’s worth emphasizing that the airline still technically has a “premium” first class, in the sense of a cabin above business class.

Specifically, American still has its specially configured Airbus A321T aircraft, which are used primarily for flights between New York (JFK) and Los Angeles (LAX) and San Francisco (SFO). The planes have 10 reverse herringbone seats spread across five rows, in a 1-1 configuration.

American also plans to eliminate this product, as the A321Ts will be reconfigured into standard A321 domestic configuration aircraft, and A321XLRs will be taking over the transcon routes.

American has stopped selling first class on these planes for flights as of March 28, 2027. After that date we’ll still see some of the planes flying with the cabins, but the first class seats will simply be sold as business class.

American Airlines has officially eliminated its international first class product, as Boeing 777-300ERs no longer have Flagship First for sale. These planes are being retrofitted, as first class seats are being eliminated, and new business class suites are being introduced. However, the planes will keep flying around with the current cabins for quite some time, and business class passengers can freely assign the first class seats.

In the spring, we’ll see American eliminate its last “premium” first class product, which is the A321T first class cabin, as those planes are replaced by A321XLRs.

What do you make of the end of American’s Flagship First on the 777?

Citi Shop takes some of the work out of saving money online. Once you've installed its browser extension, it acts as a shopping portal and coupon hunter all-in-one, rewarding you with statement credits.

It has broad reach, too, with more than 5,000 participating online merchants. That's easier than a traditional online shopping portal, which requires you to remember to start at the portal and click through before filling your cart.

Its ease of use makes it a great resource, but other portals or special discounts may save you more.

Here's how Citi Shop works and what to consider to determine if it's the best savings path for you.

Citi Shop is a free browser extension for primary cardholders with an eligible Citi credit card, including ThankYou points cards and cobranded cards. Citi retail and commercial cards are usually ineligible.

Offers come as either a percentage back or a fixed amount back, and your earnings are applied as a statement credit on the Citi card you selected during enrollment.

Citi Shop is separate from Citi Merchant Offers, which requires you to enroll in targeted offers with a specific Citi card and then use that card for the qualifying purchase.

Both Citi Shop and traditional portals give you an extra reward for making purchases they track.

But Citi Shop brings potential rebates to you, rather than requiring you to initiate your savings search. The extension automatically displays a pop-up with an available offer when you visit a participating website. You'll have the option to activate the offer before checkout.

All of Citi Shop's rebates are provided as statement credits, unlike the potential airline miles, hotel points or credit card rewards of traditional portals.

What I like about Citi Shop is that it also acts like a shopping assistant. Instead of opening six coupon sites only to discover that every code expired last Tuesday, it handles the scavenger hunt for you and tests available promo codes on your behalf.

Like Capital One Shopping, Citi Shop uses a browser extension. However, Capital One Shopping doesn't require a Capital One card to enroll and its rewards can be redeemed for eligible gift cards instead of a statement credit.

Generally speaking, Citi Shop clashes with other shopping portals. Both work by referring and tracking your purchase, so they can be mutually exclusive. You'll need to make your purchase through whichever offer is better.

Related: Chase shopping portal guide: How to earn bonus Ultimate Rewards points

Unless Citi Shop finds a promo code, it won't lower your total at checkout. Its returns arrive later as statement credits and may require patiently waiting two to six months, sometimes longer.

Even though you need an eligible Citi card to enroll, you don’t have to pay with it. Citi allows any payment method accepted by the merchant.

I really appreciate the flexibility to choose the best card for each purchase. For electronics, I might pick a card with an extended warranty while I might stick to a travel rewards credit card for hotel bookings. You can even pay with a gift card if you wish.

Regardless of how you pay, the statement credit will post to the Citi card you enrolled.

If you have an eligible Citi card but rarely remember to click through a shopping portal, Citi Shop is an easy win. Install it, activate offers when the pop-up appears and let the credits come to you. That convenience can also be a big benefit if you have partners or other family members who aren't as motivated to strategize on rewards as you are.

But with a little extra effort, you might be able to earn even more. When the Citi Shop pop-up appears with an offer, take a minute to compare before you click Activate.

Checking a shopping portal aggregator such as Cashback Monitor shows payouts from multiple cash-back, airline and credit card portals, making it easier to compare a Citi Shop statement credit with points or miles elsewhere.

Suppose a $200 jacket is marked down to $160. Citi Shop finds a $10 coupon, bringing the checkout price to $150, and offers 8% back. Assuming the full amount qualifies, you'd receive a $12 Citi Shop credit. If you pay with a card that earns 2% back and has an activated merchant offer for $5 off a $100 purchase, you'd collect another $8. After all the credits and rewards post, your net cost would be $130.

Read the terms before getting too excited. Some brands, products, gift cards or coupon codes may be excluded and you might not be able to stack every layer every time. Still, you can often use multiple discounts simultaneously for a better deal.

Citi Shop is not a program for instant gratification. Citi says statement credits post 61 to 180 days after a completed purchase, though some can take longer.

In many cases, offers may show as pending long before they officially pay out, to account for potential returns. Hotel rewards may remain pending until after the stay. Eventually, you'll see it on your statement as "CITI SHOP STATEMENT CREDIT."

If a credit hasn't posted after the expected window, contact Citi using the number on the back of your enrolled card. You may want to keep good records along the way, like a screenshot of the offer and an e-receipt from the purchase.

Citi Shop's biggest advantage is convenience. It does the heavy lifting by reminding you to activate offers so you don't miss out on earnings from your online orders, while testing coupon codes along the way. The offers themselves may or may not be the highest available, but they are certainly the easiest.

To truly optimize your returns, you'll want to compare Citi Shop earnings with those from other shopping portals — and stack other forms of saving along the way. But when that sounds like too much, the ease of this extension can still be a great way to tack on some extra returns.

#6172. The True Cost Airbus Charges For An A330neo Compared With Boeing's 787-9 Dreamliner

The Airbus A330-900 (A330neo) and the Boeing 787-9 Dreamliner are very close competitors. On the face of it, the 787-9 has a much larger order book (1,493 vs 511), has a noticeably higher market value, and is a cleansheet aircraft. This could be interpreted as suggesting the 787-9 has a cost advantage over the A330-900. However, the truth is more complicated, and it allows the A330-900 to remain competitive.

As Simple Flying has previously highlighted, headline list figures are an unreliable method to determine the true costs and value of aircraft and aero engines. To faithfully answer the headline of this article, list prices need to be set aside in favor of market prices and lease rates. The aviation industry runs on very thin margins. Consequently, averaging the costs of these two aircraft without considering the contingent variables of the airline in question will likely provide highly misleading numbers.

To understand why list prices are not particularly useful, it is necessary to understand what they are. An aircraft manufacturer’s list price is the published, baseline 'sticker price' for a new aircraft before negotiated discounts, rebates, or custom configuration changes. These are typically inflated prices where the manufacturer is essentially saying, "this is what we value our product at," even though it realistically never sells them at that price and airlines and lessors would never pay it.

For an analogy, think of an airline offering the chance to win a holiday package "valued at $10,000." That figure may include estimates for tours, accommodation, flights, transfers, etc., all priced at the highest retail price. In practice, the airline would likely be utilizing spare capacity, receiving bulk discounts, and having special pricing arrangements, so it's only paying a fraction of the headline figure.

Likewise, holidaymakers may be able to book their own analogous trip at a fraction of the cost. List prices are similar, although they may provide a starting point in complex aircraft negotiations. As discussed below, sometimes the airplane manufacturer (Airbus, Boeing) has significant bargaining power in negotiations, while at other times the balance can swing to the customer (e.g., Emirates vis-à-vis the 777-9).

Currently, the market values for Boeing 787-9s and A330neos are unusually high due to production bottlenecks at Airbus and Boeing. IBA writes, "This has pushed the expected delivery dates for many recent orders as far back as early 2030. With hampered production rates, it comes as no surprise that this has, in turn, allowed for Market Values and MLRs to rally over the years." The value of widebody aircraft has grown especially fast over the last year.

In a November 2026 update, IBA reported, "Constrained supply is supporting trading values, with 2026 market values up 7% for the 787-9, 5% for the A350-900, 24% for the 777-300ER and 20% for the A330-300, alongside rising lease rates." This shows a significant increase in market value for the older A330-300 cousin to the A330neo, but fails to include the A330neo price increase.

Cost comparison (per IBA, My Air Trade, Green Airlines)

While it's unclear how much the A330-900's market value has increased recently, its market lease rates are up by as much as 13%. The monthly market lease rate for a new Boeing 787-9 Dreamliner is around $1.05-$1.16 million, and around $900,000-$990,000 for the A330neo. At mid-age, the 787-9's rate is around $695,000-$792,000, while the A330neo is around $600,000-$756,000 per month.

The aircraft had an impressive impact on the market.

In Q1 2026, for a newly delivered Airbus A330-900, IBA ascribed a market value of $118.5 million. Meanwhile, a new Boeing 787-9 is expected to trade in the region of $160 million. Overall, the new-delivery market value of a Boeing 787-9 is estimated to be in the $151–$160 million range by different industry analysts. The new-delivery market value range of an A330-900 (A330neo) is around $118.5–$119 million.

For comparison, the market value for larger 787-10 new-builds is around $168 million, or about $8 million more than the standard 787-9. The new value of the short 787-8 is around $116 million, or almost the same as a new A330-900. My Air Trade shows that the oldest 787-9 is estimated at around $70.6 million, while the oldest A330-900 is valued at around $73 million.

The oldest second-hand examples are estimated to be $47 million for the 787-8 and $95 million for the 787-10. No market values are given for the unpopular A330-800 variant, perhaps due to the limited deliveries and lack of market trading for the aircraft. Separately, the market values for the A380 are very low. The oldest A380s are estimated to be worth $12 million, and the most valuable are around $45 million. Put another way, a new A330-900 is worth around 3x-10x that of the world's remaining A380s.

The A330-900 and Boeing 787-9 compete on the market for a similar (but not the same) market segment. These aircraft are similar in length and have comparable typical 3-class seating capacities: 260-300 for the A330-900 and 250-290 for the 787-9. The maximum seating is around 460 and 420, respectively. In practice, the 787-9s are typically assigned more to flagship routes than the A330neo and are configured with an average of 264 seats, compared with the A330-900's denser 281-seat average.

They have almost identical maximum take-off weights (251 tonnes vs 254 tonnes) and are both very competitive in terms of cargo capacity. The Boeing 787-9 is deemed to have a modest advantage in range, although that only matters in edge cases, as most missions are well within the A330neo's maximum range. When it comes to fuel burn, it depends heavily on payload, configuration, and range. As a rule, the 787-9's fuel advantage grows with longer ranges.

One of the biggest differences is that the 787-9 is a fundamentally cleansheet composite aircraft, while the A330neo is a comprehensive update on the 1980s-designed A330. The A330neo has new engines, new wings, new avionics, and other updates, but it still has an older architecture and a mostly aluminum fuselage.

The Airbus A330neo and Boeing 787-9 were developed using different design philosophies, and the contrast is particularly clear in their wings.

It is impossible to put a precise figure on how much the A330-900 and 787-9 cost to operate relative to each other. Too much is contingent. Even setting aside that these aircraft are better optimized for different routes and missions, many airline-specific factors matter. One important factor is the composition of the airline's overall fleet.

If an airline (e.g., Delta) also operates older A330s and new A350s, it can significantly increase fleet commonality and significantly reduce maintenance and training expenses. Airbus claims up to 95% commonality in A330ceo/A330neo spare parts, including substantial tooling commonality and the same pilot type rating between the generations. Airbus also claims, "Today, the A321neo and the A330neo have proven to deliver up to 30% lower operating costs when operated together."

By contrast, the benefits of commonality are more limited with airlines operating the Boeing 777 and Boeing 787, with no common type rating and the 787 requiring dedicated tooling. Commonality with the predecessor Boeing 767 is even more limited. However, there is a very high benefit to operating parallel fleets of 787-8s and 787-10s. The value of commonality can drive major airlines (e.g., Southwest, Ryanair) to only operate one family of aircraft.

As shown by the market prices, the A330-900 is around $30–40 million cheaper in new aircraft value and has a lower lease rate per month. This suggests the A330-900 benefits from lower capital, financing, and leasing costs. But this hides a major distortion. This is the secondary-market value, not the cost at which they were purchased. The largest order (cumulative) for the A330-900 is by Cathay Pacific for 41, while the largest cumulative order for the 787-9 is 132 by United (and 221 for all Boeing 787 variants).

As a general rule, an airline purchasing aircraft in the single digits may be in a negotiating position to get around 25% off the list price (with massive variation). An airline ordering 50–100 aircraft could be able to negotiate a 45–55% discount off the list price. These purchase price differences disappear once they hit the secondary market.

In practice, airlines can bundle orders, as when Qatar Airways ordered 130 Dreamliners and 30 Boeing 777-9s with options for 50 Boeing 787/777X airliners. All this is to say that the cost of operating an A330-900 may be higher or lower than that of the 787-9, depending on the circumstances. Using some back-of-the-envelope math, both airliners will likely cost around $13,000 per flight hour to operate, plus or minus a few thousand dollars. The winner will be highly contingent.

#6171. Some records in Ilhan Omar case will be released, judge says

Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., speaks during a news conference at the Capitol last summer. Few details have emerged so far about the government’s search of her home earlier this fall. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

A judge said he will order the release of some information about the federal investigation into Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., which included a search of her Washington house last month.

Judge James Boasberg for the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia made the statement Tuesday during a hearing brought by news organizations and an advocacy group seeking details about the search. Boasberg ordered the government to provide him by Friday what could be disclosed in the case. He pointed to how investigators are handling the “speech or debate” clause immunity that Omar has as a sitting member of Congress.

“This is purely legal questions, interesting questions, about the privilege, the extent of the privilege and how it would apply,” Boasberg said.

The Constitution includes an immunity for members of Congress for the “speech or debate” they engage in as part of their jobs.

Boasberg also directed the government to propose redactions to the as-yet secret docket. While he said next week’s expected disclosures would not include the 67-page document that investigators provided to justify the search, he left the door open to unsealing that down the road if the government closes the case or brings charges.

Justice Department attorney Alessandra Serano argued against broad disclosures, calling it “very rare that a precharging, pre-indictment unsealing would happen.”

The high-profile nature of the investigation leaked into the courtroom Tuesday, as Boasberg cited statements by President Donald Trump and others about the investigation into Omar.

“You have had administration officials, prominent ones, talking about the purpose of the investigation,” Boasberg said.

Administration officials have accused Omar of committing immigration crimes for years, and Trump said last month the DOJ was looking into Omar “strongly.” Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said on a recent podcast that investigators had served multiple search warrants and were investigating possible immigration fraud tied to when Omar entered the United States as a child.

Separately, Boasberg said he may issue rulings in the coming weeks unsealing portions of other court cases tied to the investigation, including one brought by Omar herself earlier this month seeking the return of the items seized in the search.

The administration executed the search warrant in October, just a few weeks before the midterm elections. The timing of the search drew accusations of political bias from Democrats who claimed that the administration brought the case to sway the midterm elections.

For years Trump has said he wanted criminal charges to be brought against his political foes, including Omar and others in Congress.

#6170. Why International First Class Has Failed At US Airlines (But Shouldn’t)

We’ve just seen American formally retire its Boeing 777 first class, and with that, no airline in the United States has a “true” international first class anymore. It’s the end of an era, because going back many decades, premium products were largely pioneered by US carriers. So I think this raises the question — why can US carriers not make first class work in a way that’s economically viable, especially as they keep talking about how premium they are?

Before we get into this, let me make sure we’re all on the same page when it comes to terms. This post isn’t about the premium cabin on domestic flights, which is often referred to as first class. Instead, it’s about international flights that have a cabin above business class, when it’s marketed as first class. So this would include airlines on my list of the world’s best first class products.

Airline executives are divided on the merits of having an international first class cabin. Some insist that there’s no need for such a cabin, as business class has improved so much. Meanwhile others absolutely see merit to such a product.

I mean, just look at how carriers like Air France, Lufthansa, Singapore Airlines, and SWISS, are all investing in first class. I think Air France’s La Premiere first class is the perfect example of the upside such a product has for an airline:

What’s interesting is that for the airlines that succeed with first class, the single biggest market — and single biggest point of sale — is the United States. So how is it that carriers like Air France, Lufthansa, SWISS, etc., can make money offering first class to the United States (primarily targeting Americans), but US airlines seemingly can’t?

The US has way too many people with tens or hundreds of millions of dollars, or even billions of dollars. There are plenty of people who would pay to fly private, and would pay for Air France La Premiere first class, but would never consider paying the high price for first class on a US carrier, because it’s just not worth it.

When they fly first class, they want this…

It’s no surprise that first class at US carriers has historically failed. In many ways, it reflects the failures of the industry from decades past. In other words, first class has long been thought of as “upgrade class,” rather than something actually worth paying for. US carriers have managed to change that narrative on domestic flights, but not so much on international flights.

What explains the failure of first class at US carriers? If you ask me, here are the main factors:

Call it a hot take, but I think international first class absolutely could succeed at a US carrier, if done right, with a couple of caveats. Let me start with the two main hurdles that would need to be overcome, and I’ll acknowledge, this might just be the biggest issue:

If those hurdles could be overcome, here’s the play, as I see it (and yes, this is largely inspired by Air France La Premiere):

I think the halo effect of something like this would be massive as well. Seriously, US airline executives love to talk about how premium they are, but they can’t even introduce a top-end product, despite having access to the most lucrative customer base in the world.

In terms of economics, let me also point out that the opportunity cost of a first class cabin isn’t actually that high. “Premium” is all the rage, so what you do here is eliminate some economy seats:

At this point, no airline from the United States offers first class on international flights anymore. For airlines that can’t stop talking about how unbelievably premium they are, I find that to be a pretty perplexing reality. I know that many people have just accepted “oh, a good business class is the future,” but I have a different take.

I think no US carrier actually being able to offer a globally competitive product is a failure in strategy and creativity. They have access to the world’s most lucrative customer base, and other airlines can seemingly make money serving US customers with a first class product. The issue is, US carriers have long not actually given people a reason to fly first class, all while offering too much capacity.

Personally I think there would be a lot of merit to an international first class product that’s boutique, and is operated in the right markets. That’s not to say that I think it’ll happen — I don’t — but I do think it could succeed. The only real hurdle to overcome would be how to ensure good service…

What’s your take on the possible merit of US carriers offering first class?

#6168. These incoming members of Congress have been here before

Rep.-elect Chris Rabb, D-Pa., greets current members of Congress in the Capitol on Nov. 11. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

When Rep.-elect Chris Rabb first worked on Capitol Hill in the 1990s, it didn’t exactly inspire him to want to go into politics.

“I said, ‘Oh, this is how the sausage is made? I should be a vegan,’” the Pennsylvania Democrat recalled.

Working for Carol Moseley Braun, the first Black woman elected as a U.S. senator, Rabb saw threats and “just vile things” directed at her.

“My entrée to service behind the scenes was seeing voluminous amounts of violence, hate speech and death threats against my boss, and I thought to myself, ‘Why would anyone want to serve?’” he said.

During his time in the state legislature starting in 2017, Rabb “fell in love with public service, despite the vitriol.” Now, the democratic socialist describes coming to Congress as “surreal,” as he succeeds retiring Rep. Dwight Evans in a deep-blue district based in West Philadelphia.

Rabb is one of more than a dozen incoming members who have worked on the Hill before, ranging from interns to chiefs of staff and everything in between.

Unlike some in the 100-plus-strong freshman class, they already know their way around the hallways. And Rabb has some advice for his new colleagues: “Treat your staff well. Take care of your staff; they’ll take care of you.”

Here are some of the former staffers who will join the House in January.

A couple years ago, Killin was working as chief of staff to former second gentleman Doug Emhoff. But she started out on the Hill.

“It is helpful to know, as I joke, where the bathrooms are, but I still feel like I have a lot to learn,” said the Army veteran, who unseated Republican Rep. Jeff Crank in a Colorado Springs-area district.

She served as the top staffer for three House Democrats: Donna Shalala of Florida, Carolyn Maloney of New York and Marie Gluesenkamp Perez of Washington.

“I’ve actually opened up two freshman offices, so it’s helpful to have done that before,” Killin said.

White will be just the third person in modern times to hold the job of nonvoting D.C. delegate. He replaces retiring Del. Eleanor Holmes Norton — also his former boss.

Before his time on the D.C. Council, he worked as her legislative counsel, watching her navigate a role with limited power in her perennial fight for statehood.

“I need to make sure I’m developing a national profile for this seat,” he said, vowing to continue the quest for full representation even as President Donald Trump seeks to exert more control over the District.

One of just a few Republican women in the freshman class, Gruters said she “never in a million years” imagined coming to Congress herself, despite her years as a staffer.

She will replace retiring Rep. Vern Buchanan in Florida’s 16th District, after once serving as his operations director. She also worked as district director for Rep. Greg Steube, R-Fla.

“I never thought this would be the path, but I’m honored to do it,” said Gruters, whose husband leads the Republican National Committee.

Rogers added another title to his résumé last week: freshman class president.

His fellow incoming Republicans tapped him for the role. Not so long ago, he was working for the Senate Judiciary Committee, fresh off a stint at the white-shoe law firm White & Case.

In 2025 he served as general counsel for Sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla., and plans to keep pushing for a bill he helped draft that aims to crack down on foreign surrogacy contracts. “We are currently selling American children to China, our No. 1 adversary,” Rogers said, describing it as “deplorable.”

Rogers will succeed retiring GOP Rep. Neal Dunn in the Florida Panhandle.

García’s run for her boss’s seat drew controversy from the start. When Rep. Jesús “Chuy” García, D-Ill., waited to publicly announce his retirement until after the filing deadline in Illinois had already passed, critics blasted him for effectively boxing out other candidates and clearing the way for his chief of staff.

He faced a rare formal disapproval vote in the House over the move. But García has insisted she is more than a hand-picked successor, saying on her campaign website that she has “delivered solutions rooted in lived experience.”

The son of Ghanaian immigrants, Boafo is a state delegate who has lobbied on the Hill for tech company Oracle.

He also worked as campaign manager for Rep. Steny H. Hoyer, earning an endorsement from the retiring longtime Democrat and campaign cash from groups aligned with him.

Boafo prevailed in a crowded primary, even as Speaker Emerita Nancy Pelosi threw her weight behind a different candidate, former Capitol Police officer Harry Dunn.

Sell worked under then-House Agriculture Chair Larry Combest during the 2000 crop insurance overhaul and the fight over the 2002 farm bill. He later joined his former boss in launching an agricultural lobbying firm, Combest, Sell and Associates.

Once a precocious child magician who wrote his own book of tricks, Lasher also got an early start in politics.

“I feel supremely fortunate to have wandered into Jerry Nadler’s political orbit as a teenager 30 years ago, and then to have worked in his congressional office a decade later,” Lasher wrote in an opinion piece for City & State New York.

Backed by the retiring Nadler, the self-described “nerd” beat out a couple of big names in the primary, including a Kennedy family heir. Another former boss endorsed him, too: Gov. Kathy Hochul. Before serving as a New York state assemblyman, Lasher worked as her policy director.

Villegas ousted GOP Rep. David Valadao in a closely watched race in the San Joaquin Valley.

A decade ago, he was an intern for Rep. John Garamendi, D-Calif. And the progressive also interned for former California state Rep. Rudy Salas, who made unsuccessful bids to unseat Valadao in 2022 and 2024.

A San Diego City councilmember, Von Wilpert flipped the seat held by Republican Rep. Darrell Issa, who decided not to run for reelection under a map redrawn by Democrats.

When she worked for the National Labor Relations Board in 2016, she was detailed to the House Education and Labor Committee, working under ranking member Robert C. Scott, D-Va.

Jackie Wang and Nick Eskow contributed to this report.

A previous version of this report misstated when Rudy Salas ran for office.

Washingtonians have a new option to Portugal next summer.

TAP Air Portugal will launch a new thrice-weekly service from Dulles International Airport (IAD) to Porto Airport (OPO) on March 30, 2027. Westbound flights will operate on Wednesdays, Fridays and Saturdays through the summer, and on Mondays, Wednesdays and Fridays beginning in October.

TAP, a Star Alliance partner of United Airlines, will fly an Airbus A321LR on the new IAD-OPO route. The long-range, single-aisle aircraft is fitted with 16 lie-flat business-class seats and 155 economy seats.

The new Portugal route is the latest international addition at IAD. United plans to launch new service to Toulouse, France, in April and to Milan in May, using its new long-range A321XLR on the former route.

International seats from IAD will increase nearly 7% in the first six months of 2027 compared to this year, schedule data from aviation analytics firm Cirium shows.

IAD is undergoing a massive, $22 billion redevelopment to bring its infrastructure up to modern standards. The first piece — a 14-gate section of the new Concourse E that includes a new, large United Club — opened earlier in November. Future phases include a new international arrivals facility that would support additional long-haul growth.

And if the redevelopment plan stays on schedule, IAD could retire its jet-age mobile lounges by the mid-2030s.

TAP’s new OPO route complements its existing service to IAD from Lisbon Airport (LIS).

The state-owned Portuguese airline is in the process of being privatized as part of the Lufthansa Group. The German airline conglomerate plans to buy an initial 44.9% stake in TAP, aiming to close the deal by the first quarter of 2028.

Lufthansa Group chief commercial officer Dieter Vranckx said in October that once the TAP deal is done, Lufthansa intends to integrate the Portuguese airline into its transatlantic joint venture with Air Canada and United.

#6166. Why Airlines Accept The Airbus A321XLR's Heavier 101.5-Tonne Maximum Takeoff Weight On Flights Shorter Than An Hour

Sergey Kohl | Shutterstock, Simple Flying

The Airbus A321XLR has helped open a new chapter in long-and-thin aviation. As the latest variant to appear in the Airbus A320 family, the XLR — or Extra Long Range — has taken the crown as the longest-range commercial narrowbody. Simply put, it has provided operators with arguably the best means yet of efficiently serving long-haul routes that would otherwise be unsuited to larger, widebody aircraft.

Despite its impressive capabilities, airlines have been known to put the XLR to work on connections that span a fraction of the distance the aircraft can actually fly. In some extreme cases, these do not even stretch to an hour of flight time. But modifications were needed for the XLR to earn its title, and these added weight. So for those opting to schedule their XLRs on such short routes, the reality is accepting the penalties of operating a heavier plane than might normally do the job. Nonetheless, carriers continue to do so anyway, which raises the question: Why?

On the surface, the A321XLR and standard Airbus A321neo appear almost identical. They share a score of common features, from their engines to their capacities to their basic dimensions, including wingspans and the same fuselage length, width, and height. A bystander could not be blamed for mistaking one for the other as a result.

Airbus deliberately developed the duo this way too, with these retained features making it operationally viable for airlines to operate both variants in their fleets. Unchanged dimensions mean the same gate spacing and ground equipment can be used at airports, for instance. It also simplifies crew training, as pilots can fly either variant without having to train for an entirely separate type rating.

Select A321XLR and A321neo specifications, from Airbus:

There are key differences between the two, which is why the XLR has a stronger range and higher maximum takeoff weight. The range is largely enabled by the addition of a permanent 3,407.82-US gallon (12,900-3liter) rear center tank on the XLR, which also explains the increased weight; Airbus has also developed an updated fuel system and outfitted the variant with necessary structural reinforcements. Ultimately, this has pushed the XLR’s maximum range to 4,700 nautical miles (8,700 km) — which is a notable step up on the NEO’s.

Because of this, any instance where an airline chooses to use the A321XLR on a short-haul hop may seem counterintuitive. Indeed, the XLR was specifically designed to increase the A320 family's top range. Even so, many airlines do use the variant for this purpose in practice.

Air Canada uses its XLRs in part to connect Ottawa Macdonald-Cartier International Airport (YOW) and Toronto Pearson International Airport (YYZ), as well as Montréal-Trudeau International Airport (YUL) and Toronto, for instance. Each of these journeys lasts roughly 39 and 53 minutes, respectively, spanning between 197 nautical miles (364 km) and 274 nautical miles (507 km). Concurrently, the carrier also services its almost nine-hour Toronto to Tenerife South Airport (TFS) route using XLRs.

Across the Atlantic, Ireland’s Aer Lingus XLRs flew more than 300 flights exceeding 3,100 miles (2,694 nautical miles or 4,989 km), alongside over 200 flights of 1,250 miles (1,086 nautical miles or 2,012 km) or fewer, in July this year, according to aviation data platform Avi-Go. These included Dublin Airport (DUB) to Nashville International Airport (BNA), scheduled at nine hours and 20 minutes, but also Dublin to London Heathrow Airport (LHR) and Dublin to Josep Tarradellas Barcelona–El Prat Airport (BCN), lasting just 48 minutes and one hour and 50 minutes, respectively. Needless to say, the XLR is by no means solely used for its range in either case.

The range and efficiency of the XLR commands a premium over other narrowbody aircraft currently on the market.

Air Canada and Aer Lingus are not alone, though. It is common practice among A321XLR operators to run the models on diverse routes with wide-ranging flight times and distances. At least, this is the case as it stands.

Based on data from aviation analyst Cirium covering last July, American Airlines, Saudia, and Wizz Air were among the handful of XLR operators that were doing just that. The former flew its XLRs on journeys spanning the 540- to 1,079-nautical mile (1,000- to 1,999-km) and 2,700 to 3,239-nautical mile (5,000- to 5,999-km) brackets, as well as everything in between. Interestingly, these figures showed Iberia — the XLR’s launch customer back in October 2024 — was the only carrier to exclusively use the variant for connections in the highest 2,700- to 3,239-nautical mile (5,000- to 5,999-km) and 3,240- to 3,779-nautical mile (6,000- to 6,999-km) brackets over the course of the month.

Airbus A321XLR operators as of mid-November:

In other words, the carrier that has had the most time to incorporate the aircraft into its fleet appeared to be the one getting the most out of the XLR’s range most frequently. That is not surprising, though, given Airbus has only begun delivering the model in the past few years. By our count, just 61 models had been delivered to 11 carriers as of the time of writing in November, out of more than 500 orders placed.

As such, those tasked with fitting the A321XLR into wider schedules have only recently benefited from the jets actually being on hand. Although orders placed years in advance will have given time to prepare, there is little replacement for real-world experience — especially since the XLR is, in many ways, unmatched by anything that has come before it.

In Iberia’s case, the XLR has appeared more capable than anticipated. “[It’s] even better than originally planned in terms of stage length,” chief executive Marco Antonio Trujillo said previously. “In fact, we are operating currently to the Caribbean, San Juan and Santo Domingo, where initially we were not thinking that the range could get over there.”

On the flip side, Air Canada had planned to introduce XLRs between Toronto and London Heathrow this year. However, the Canadian flag carrier pulled the type before it could even debut on the service, instead opting to stick with narrowbodies for the time being. All of this goes to say, planning in advance is one thing, but meeting operational requirements in real time can be another story altogether.

The aircraft offers game-changing capabilities.

This can also explain why widebodies are sometimes used for surprisingly short journeys. Where the A321XLR’s capacity makes it an ideal, like-for-like replacement for other narrowbodies and the A321neo in particular, sometimes that is not even enough.

Several short-haul services this year were scheduled to be flown by widebodies, as flagged by industry publication Aerospace Global News, which are traditionally associated with long-haul routes. Not least, the Airbus A350 — itself known for carrying out the longest flights on offer today — was deployed on several intra-European flights, as shown below. Similarly, the double-decker Airbus A380 saw use within Asia on a sub-six-hour connection that would technically fail to qualify as long-haul by definition.

Select widebody-operated short-haul routes scheduled for this year, from Aerospace Global News:

As to why such huge aircraft are selected for flights that do not quite match up to their capabilities, there are several reasons. Demand, for example, may call for more seats and make a bigger jet the more viable option. Airport slot constraints may similarly play a part, leaving airlines having to move greater numbers of passengers at once. The same factors apply to the XLR, which is designed to offer carriers a lower-risk alternative when demand isn't there to support running a widebody. No doubt, that also stretches to opening up new so-called long and thin routes, although discovering these will take time, as we are seeing today.

At the core of all the decision-making as to which aircraft to use on which route, when and how often, and so on, is the simple fact that a plane sitting out of action on the ground is a plane not generating revenue. Whether it's a narrowbody or a widebody, using it is better than leaving it idle while waiting for the perfect deployment. Add in factors such as demand, and the reasons an aircraft type may not appear to match the route distance pile up.

In the case of the A321XLR, Airbus has created a model as impressive for its flexibility as it is for its range. Yes, it can match several widebodies in distance, replacing them if needed due to lackluster demand. It can also fill in or complement fellow narrowbodies when required, thanks to its commonality with the A321neo.

The caveat is the weight penalty, which is most noticeable on shorter routes. Nonetheless, airlines have clearly deemed it an acceptable trade-off to keep both their routes and jets active, and thus generating revenue in turn.

#6165. Why I’d Pick Economy Over Premium Economy On An Overnight Flight

I just got back to Rio after a quick trip to Ireland for Aer Lingus’ event to showcase their new A330 cabins, including its first-ever premium economy.

I flew Air France economy both ways, and I’m glad I resisted the offer of $420 during online check-in to upgrade the outbound overnight economy leg. Ironically, it was the long day-flight back where I actually wished I’d upgraded.

However, to answer the economy vs. premium economy question, it all comes down to maximising comfort, and I think this is easier to do in economy than premium economy.

If, like me, sleeping upright or on your back is almost impossible, then what follows will likely apply to you.

The main reason I’m deterred to pick premium economy for overnight flights is because of the fixed armrests, where tray tables are sometimes stowed in this cabin.

Despite the extra recline and leg rest element (which sometimes makes it even harder to get comfortable), the fixed armrests restrict the ability to sleep any way other than straight like a pencil.

To make matters worse, they stop you from lying across more than one seat if you find yourself in an empty row.

It’s for that reason that I much prefer economy. While having a row to yourself isn’t guaranteed, there’s at least a chance of being able to move around the cabin, or stretch out into an empty seat. No matter where you sit or how empty the cabin is, you can’t do that in premium economy.

Another element of my pre-trip planning that I expect many of you to relate to is the fact it takes me so long umming and aahing over the best seat to pick.

Thanks to my Flying Blue Gold status (SkyTeam Elite Plus), I could pick any seat in the economy cabin of the Boeing 777-200ER for free from 72 hours before departure.

I narrowed it down to an empty seat in the exit row, and the only row of three with an empty middle seat. I didn’t even consider one of the many empty middle rows of four seats in case they filled up before take off and I ended up in an aisle with no window to rest my head. Using the window or plane’s fuselage to rest my head on is the only saving grace for me when trying to sleep sitting upright.

As the empty exit seat would have the same restricting fixed partition as premium, I decided against that, too.

After the “boarding complete” announcement was made, the middle seat in my row remained empty, and there were three seats free in the middle of row 25, a row in front. I explained to the girl in the aisle seat that if one of us moved to the other row, we’d both have three seats to ourselves. She didn’t seem to understand my point, and said she’d prefer to sit in the aisle than us both have three free seats to ourselves.

I didn’t want to move to the middle seats either, so I got as comfortable as I could using the middle seat and the pillow I brought from home.

In the end, I did manage to get some half decent curled up shut eye (the thick pillow protected my back from the hard parts of the seat when propped against the fuselage). However, when I went to the loo, I noticed some people in the rear cabin had got lucky and were fast asleep spread across a whole four seats.

Maybe I’ll take more of a risk next time…

I’m not saying economy is always a better choice than premium. For example, I’d always recommend Emirates’ pretty darn impressive premium economy over economy, because it genuinely is several steps up from economy.

If it was up to me, I’d have had a lie-flat seat for the overnight segment. I didn’t, and I’m pretty certain I got better sleep quality curled up across two seats in economy that I would have almost upright on my back in premium.

Would you ever choose economy over premium economy?

#6164. Zinke PAC gave to family foundation he was investigated for

Rep. Ryan Zinke, R-Mont., leaves a meeting of the House Republican Conference at the Capitol Hill Club on July 15, 2025. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

Outgoing Montana GOP Rep. Ryan Zinke gave $200,000 in campaign cash to a family foundation headed by his wife that was once at the center of a federal investigation and an ethics scandal that led him to resign as Interior secretary in 2019.

The gift, which has not previously been reported, was made on Aug. 31 from Zinke’s leadership political action committee to the nonprofit Great Northern Veterans Peace Foundation, campaign finance records show. The donation is more than the foundation has reported receiving in any year since it was founded nearly two decades ago.

Zinke’s wife, son, and sister currently serve on its board of directors, according to the foundation’s annual filing with the state of Montana.

In a brief interview, Zinke denied that any portion of the money transferred to the foundation will directly benefit him or any of his family members who sit on the board of directors. “No, no, never," he said when asked if any family members will draw a salary from the gift.

The money will instead go to building a storage barn and kid’s sledding park on the property controlled by the foundation, Zinke said.

None of the records indicate Zinke violated the law or directly benefited from the gift to his foundation.

“While it's not uncommon for a politician to transfer leftover money from a political war chest to charity, it is pretty rare for a politician to transfer leftover political funds to a charity that they or a relative controls,” said Michael Beckel, director of money in politics reform at Issue One, a bipartisan group that seeks to reduce influence of money in politics.

Instead, outgoing members typically transfer remaining campaign cash to local party committees or candidates, Beckel added.

Ethics experts say Zinke’s move highlights ongoing concerns over the broad latitude campaign finance law gives leadership PACs in how they spend money.

“I definitely think it is something to be concerned about,” said Stuart McPhail, director of campaign finance litigation at Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington, a nonprofit watchdog.

“Leadership PACs are really nothing more than personal slush funds under today's rules,” he said, noting that unlike regular campaign committees, member leadership PACs are not prohibited from donating to charities or organizations that could directly benefit the member or relative.

Zinke, a former Navy SEAL who commanded special forces during the Iraq War, converted his traditional campaign committee to a leadership PAC — Commander Zinke Leadership Fund — in March 2026, shortly after announcing he would not run for reelection. It last reported having $1.4 million cash on hand in October of this year.

It marks the second time one of Zinke’s political committees made a payment to the organization. In 2019, the committee Zinke ran during his earlier years in Congress — he served one term in the House before being tapped as Trump’s first-term Interior secretary — gave over $11,000 to the foundation before winding down operations.

The Great Northern Veterans Peace Foundation was founded by Zinke and his wife in 2007 in his hometown of Whitefish, Mont., with plans to provide winter recreational activities for children. Its latest tax filing reports revenue of $15,000 and roughly equal expenses in 2024 for snow plowing and park maintenance.

Zinke’s dealings with the organization were the subject of an ongoing inspector general investigation when he resigned as Interior secretary in January 2019.

Investigators ultimately did not find that Zinke violated conflict-of-interest laws, but they concluded that he failed to comply with federal ethics obligations and “misused his official position in violation of federal regulations.” The Justice Department declined to prosecute Zinke.

Zinke stepped down from the foundation in 2017, shortly after his Senate confirmation. But investigators found that he continued to represent the organization in negotiations with the developers of a commercial project adjacent to the foundation’s land and lied to an ethics agent about his involvement in the project.

The project’s investors included David Lesar, then-chairman of oil services company Halliburton.

Another Zinke-tied leadership PAC has previously raised eyebrows in Washington.

Supporting Electing American Leaders PAC — known as SEAL PAC — where Zinke serves as chairman, has been marred by accusations that it funneled money to political consultants instead of candidates. A 2022 CQ Roll Call analysis found that 87 percent of the PAC’s spending went to operating expenses.

The PAC also made recurring monthly payments to a company registered to Zinke’s son, Wolfgang Zinke, and based at a Zinke family-owned home in Whitefish.

SEAL PAC’s executive director, Rob Catron, maintained that the payments constitute a consulting fee to Wolfgang Zinke for management of the PAC website, among other tasks. “He earns every penny of it,” Catron said.

Since May 2022, the PAC has given roughly $270,000 to Wolfgang Zinke’s company, FG Solutions, for mailing and printing, records show — more than any individual candidate or committee supported by the PAC. The company also received $5,000 from a related super PAC, SEAL PAC USA, which can solicit unlimited contributions for independent expenditures but can’t donate directly to candidates.

Montana corporate records show Wolfgang Zinke founded FG Solutions – which says it provides services including “personal assistant and any lawful purpose” – just 10 days before it received its first payment from the PAC in 2022.

Catron defended how the PAC spends money on veterans running for the House, arguing that it takes money to raise money.

“We raise a lion’s share of our funding through national direct mail fundraising, which is very expensive to do,” he said, citing the PAC’s use of a national text message fundraising campaign as a major expense.

SEAL PAC raised about $9.6 million this election cycle, distributing about $1.1 million to GOP lawmakers and candidates, according to Federal Election Commission filings. Most of the committee's funds went to operating expenses, including over $3 million paid to Direct Support Services, a Washington-based vendor, for direct mail postage.

Zinke’s not the only lawmaker to face scrutiny over how they spent surplus campaign cash in recent years.

In 2023, Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., set off alarm bells for transferring $200,000 from his campaign committee to The Sanders Institute, a nonprofit founded by his wife and stepson, following a $350,000 donation from his 2020 presidential campaign coffers.

The organization briefly shut down during Sanders’ presidential run in 2019 to avoid the appearance of impropriety.

Sanders’ stepson, David Driscoll — a former executive at Nike and snowboard manufacturer Burton — is listed on the think tank’s website as its executive director, drawing a six-figure annual salary according to tax filings.

It’s unusual, though not unheard of, for campaign committees to pay family members of the candidate for bona fide work.

“If [Wolfgang Zinke] is actually performing this work, he’s qualified to do it, and this is his typical market rate for this kind of contract, then it would be permissible, even if this was a campaign account,” McPhail said about SEAL PAC's payments.

But the payments could present a legal “gray area” over whether personal-use restrictions apply to certain PACs, according to McPhail.

#6163. Third Time’s Not The Charm: A SWISS A220’s Odd Triple Aborted Takeoff

If you’re a frequent flyer, odds are that you’ve encountered an aborted takeoff, whereby the plane accelerates down the runway, only to slow down, and eventually come to a stop. In some cases this can feel like a non-event, while in other cases it can feel much scarier, depending on the speed at which the takeoff is aborted.

However, here’s something you don’t often see — a SWISS Airbus A220 aborted its takeoff three times in a row, before finally returning to the gate to see what was going on, as reported by Blick. The explanation is actually quite logical, but that doesn’t make the whole ordeal any less unusual.

On Tuesday, November 17, 2026, SWISS flight LX2110 was scheduled to operate from Zurich (ZRH) to Malaga (AGP), with a 9:35AM departure. The flight was operated by an Airbus A220-300 with the registration code HB-JCM.

The plane pushed back and taxied out to the runway right on schedule. The pilots began the takeoff roll, but then quickly applied the brakes, causing the plane to come to a stop, while still at a slow speed. The pilots took a moment to run checklists, and then decided on another takeoff attempt, only for the same thing to happen again!

After the second aborted takeoff, the captain reportedly informed passengers that the thrust levers had popped out during the takeoff roll, and that was the reason for the aborted takeoff. However, rather than returning to the gate, they decided to attempt an additional takeoff roll.

Once again, the takeoff was aborted. At that point the captain explained that nothing like this had ever happened to him before in his 12 year career, and that the plane would be returning to the gate.

There ended up being a plane change, and then the A220 with the registration code HB-JCO was assigned to operate this flight — it ended up taking off at 1:29PM and landing at 3:52PM, around 3.5 hours behind schedule.

A SWISS spokesperson confirmed the incident happened, though noted that the takeoffs were aborted at a low speed of around 50 kilometers per hour (around 30 miles per hour).

What explains the aborted takeoffs? Well, it was because as the plane accelerated for takeoff, the automatic thrust control system automatically deactivated. To explain this as simply as possible, as I understand it, on the A220 when the auto-thrust is armed and the thrust levers are moved forward for takeoff, the auto-thrust then takes over, and moves the levers forward without manual intervention.

In other words, one of the pilots keeps their hands on the auto-thrust levers and “moves” with them, but doesn’t actually apply any force. Pilots are trained this way, and to not manually apply force. In the event that the crew tries to stop the auto-thrust lever motion, a pressure switch detects this, and then disengages the auto-thrust, to allow for a manual override.

In this case, the auto-thrust incorrectly detected resistance, when the pilots weren’t attempting to apply it. According to the airline, the system that monitors the aircraft’s technical status in real time was unable to identify the cause of the error, as no errors were displayed in the system. So at first, the pilots likely wondered if they had accidentally applied force.

However, once technicians had a look at the plane, it was discovered that the switch for disabling the automatic thrust control on the original aircraft was stuck, and this caused the automatic thrust control to shut down during takeoff attempts.

So while this can understandably seem scary to passengers, this wasn’t even a direct safety issue. After all, the pilots could’ve also manually moved the throttles. However, you also don’t want to take off when you know there’s an issue with the throttles, since that’s not exactly a best practice.

A SWISS Airbus A220 attempted a takeoff from Zurich three times in a row. While I’ve had two consecutive aborted takeoffs, I’ve never had three, and I can’t imagine that happens all too often.

While this is unusual, it sounds like this was handled well, and I can see why the pilots kept trying. This wasn’t a critical safety issue, but instead, just an incorrect detection of inputs, in a way that wouldn’t really pose a risk to the flight. At the same time, you don’t want to knowingly take off with a fault switch.

What do you make of this SWISS aborted takeoff trio?

The best cruise lines for families allow parents and kids to have fun together and apart while taking the stress out of group travel.

Our favorite family ships mix wow-factor activities with attractive kids clubs, plentiful and convenient dining and thoughtful touches like bathtubs and babysitting.

Your family might be happy anywhere there’s a beach or pool, but if you want an at-sea family vacation you’ll always remember, book a sailing with one of our top five cruise lines for families.

No one will be surprised that entertainment juggernaut Disney offers an amazing family cruise experience.

Disney Cruise Line ships are known for meet-and-greets with Mickey Mouse and Disney princesses, interactive movie-themed dining experiences and enormous kids clubs and play areas.

What might surprise the uninitiated is how good the line is at taking care of the whole family, not just the Mouse-obsessed little ones.

Disney thinks of all the little things that can help parents have a stress-free trip with kids in tow. From split bathrooms (allowing one family member to take a bath while another uses the toilet) to waiters who will cut up your child’s food, Disney Cruise Line takes the pressure off parents.

While other cruise lines limit water play to kids who are toilet trained and drop-off child care to ages 3 and up, Disney caters to all kids with onboard splash areas and nurseries for kids ages 6 months to 3 years.

Kids ages 3 to 10 live it up in the expansive Oceaneer Club, with attractions like an interactive replica of Star Wars’ Millennium Falcon and a play area designed to look like Andy’s Room from “Toy Story.”

Teens might roll their eyes at the ever-present Mickeys, but Disney Cruise Line does not ignore its older kid guests. Tweens and teens get their own cool hangouts, Edge (ages 11 to 14) and Vibe (ages 14 to 17), with video games, foosball and seating areas.

Additionally, first-run movies and Broadway-caliber musicals, waterslides, teen spa treatments and grab-and-go food options (and free room service) keep older kids busy and happy.

Sister ships Disney Wish, Disney Treasure and Disney Destiny feature Hero Zone sports areas for free play and competitions attractive to this age group. (Keep an eye out for the Disney Believe, too, debuting in late 2027.)

Grownups on Disney get to play as hard as they parent. Ships offer adults-only pool decks and restaurants, a nightlife scene and couples spa treatments to revive exhausted parents who haven't had a date in months.

The only caveat is that Disney Cruise Line is the most expensive cruise line on this list. At press time, seven-night Caribbean cruises start at $3,180 per person.

Related: These are the best cruise ships for kids

With some of the biggest ships at sea and an amusement park-like private island in the Bahamas, Royal Caribbean is one of the best cruise lines for active families.

Want to try surfing, sky diving, rock climbing, laser tag, bumper cars or zip lining? Families don’t have to leave the ship to find their adrenaline highs.

Even the sedentary pursuits are high-octane on Royal Caribbean. Broadway musicals, festive parades, water acrobatic performances and ice skating shows wow the crowds in the evenings and on sea days.

Expansive play spaces for kids includedrop-off nurseries for babies (ages 6 to 36 months) and Adventure Ocean for kids ages 3 to 12 (often broken into separate activities for kids ages 3 to 5, 6 to 8, and 9 to 12) with science labs and art studios on the biggest ships. Teens and tweens ages 13 to 17 get their own cool hangouts, often with activities scheduled around the ship.

While the kids live it up at cruise camp, parents can sneak off to the adults-only solarium or thermal suite.

After a hard day of play, worn-out families can refuel at a variety of restaurants, including burger and milkshake mecca Johnny Rockets, Italian and Mexican eateries and an all-day buffet.

Family cabins and connecting staterooms give larger families their needed space. The Ultimate Family Suite (and similar Ultimate Family Townhouses on some of the line’s biggest ships) can sleep eight to 10 people, and parents and kids alike might be tempted to stay up late playing air hockey, scrambling up the climbing wall, soaking in the private outdoor hot tub or watching the giant TV.

Royal Caribbean’s biggest ships – Icon, Star, and Legend of the Seas – also offers an entire section of the ship devoted to family-friendly accommodations and an outdoor dining-and-play space targeted at parents with young children.

Families should keep an eye out for kids-sail-free deals on select departures, which allow kids ages 12 and younger to pay no cruise fare when they sail as the third or fourth guest in a cabin with two full-fare-paying adults. (Note that families will still have to pay taxes, fees and port charges for kids sailing free.)

Fares for Royal Caribbean cruises can vary based on ship, and its newest, biggest ships often command premium pricing. Seven-night Caribbean cruises start from $444 per person on an older ship, but cost more than $1,000 per person on its biggest Icon Class ships.

Related: These are the best cruises for teens

Practicalities first: Carnival Cruise Line is an affordable and convenient cruise line for families who don’t live the jet-set lifestyle. With home ports all around the U.S., Carnival puts its ships within driving distance of many Americans.

A variety of short-cruise destinations, affordable-yet-spacious inside cabins (some that sleep up to four people) and lots of onboard attractions and restaurants included in the fares combine to make it one of the best value cruise lines afloat.

Carnival doesn’t dub its fleet the Fun Ships for nothing. The whole family will have a blast on board, whether you like getting down to live music, busting a gut at family-friendly comedy shows, being soaked at an onboard water park or eating green eggs and ham with Dr. Seuss characters.

The cruise line also embraces simple pleasures like free-flowing soft-serve ice cream and pizza and a day spent lounging by the pool.

Families don’t need to pull out their wallets to feed ravenous teens or sugar-fueled children. Guy Fieri burgers and barbecue, burritos for breakfast and lunch and Shaquille O’Neal’s fried chicken are all included in your cruise fares. No one’s going to make you dress up for dinner, either.

Carnival ships have plenty of cabins that can sleep four or five passengers, but six of its newerst ships truly treat families right. Book a Family Harbor cabin or suite on Vista or Excel Class ships and get access to a family lounge stocked with all the essentials — snacks and coffee, games, Wi-Fi, movies and a concierge to make bookings so mom and dad can spend more time playing with the kids.

Seven-night Caribbean cruises start at $443 per person.

It might not be a household name yet, but any cruise line that has a partnership with Lego should be on every family’s radar,  so MSC Cruises is a line families should know.

As the Mediterranean line grows its U.S.-based fleet, it's adding newer and bigger family-friendly ships to more home ports, including Miami, Port Canaveral, Galveston and Seattle.

MSC World America, the line’s newest and biggest ship sailing the Caribbean, features the Family Aventura district, a hub for kids and their grownups. It features The Harbour, an outdoor space with a ropes course, waterpark, playground and 11-deck-long dry slide; indoor sports area for family games and bumper cars; and an enormous Doremiland kids club.

Speaking of kids clubs, MSC’s ships offer play spaces for babies, kids, tweens and teens. Its ships not only offer a drop-off Baby Club (ages 6 months to 3 years) with educational toys by Chicco but also a special baby laundry service to take care of that pile of dirty onesies.

MSC divides young cruisers into Mini Club (ages 3 to 6), Junior Club (ages 7 to 11) and Young Club (12 to 14). Kids club activities go beyond arts and crafts and video games to include cooking events, sports competitions and high-tech interactive games. Teens (ages 15 to 17) can sing karaoke, dance at the onboard disco and attend themed parties with their new friends.

Outside of the kids club, families can race in a Formula One simulator, experience virtual reality, be soaked in a water park or brave their fear of heights on a suspension bridge.

Several MSC Cruises ships offer thrill rides that will appeal to all ages of adventurous cruisers. MSC Seascape features Robotron, a three-seat robotic amusement ride and MSC World America and MSC World Atlantic (coming late 2027) have the Cliffhanger, an overwater swing ride – both are hits with thrill-seeking families.

Multigenerational groups can choose connecting cabins for more space, but families keen on rooming together can take advantage of frequent "kids sail free" fares and pay only the taxes and fees for children under 18 who are the third and fourth passengers in a cabin. Seven-night Caribbean cruises start from $299 per person.

Norwegian Cruise Line is all about giving cruisers options to create different versions of the perfect cruise vacation, all within the same ship.

The flexibility and choice make it one of the best cruise lines for families, especially those who need to satisfy diverse interests or who are easily bored with the same activities day after day.

Kids clubs and adults-only sundecks allow for age-appropriate fun time apart, but Norwegian wants families to have fun together. Its Splash Academy engages kids ages 3 to 12 with group activities like team challenges and crafts, while Entourage is the place for teens ages 13 to 17 to make friends, hang out playing foosball and video games or show off their moves during evening dance parties. Adults can hide out in the 18+ Vibe Beach Club and Spice H2O for some sunbathing and hot tub time while the kids are engaged in youth activities.

Norwegian also wants families to have fun together. Teaming up to solve a murder mystery, mastering a ropes course, singing along to a high-energy musical show or live concert or screaming down a waterslide are guaranteed to create those unbreakable family bonds.

Norwegian’s flexible dining system and a plethora of onboard eateries let families plan meals to suit their schedules and tastes.

Also, free kids meals at extra-charge restaurants mean parents can sample Brazilian, Japanese, French or seafood dishes while the littles gobble up pasta and chicken fingers. Casual all-day options suit fussy eaters who need unfussy dining areas.

The cruise line also gets a shoutout for its family-friendly Hawaii itineraries. As the only big-ship cruise line that sails weeklong itineraries round trip from Honolulu, Norwegian provides an easy way for families to visit multiple islands.

Beach time, boat rides, water sports, luaus and volcano tours combine for an epic family trip, with the ship taking the stress out of meals and transportation.

In the Bahamas, Norwegian’s enhanced Great Stirrup Cay private island now features a waterpark with a variety of slides, a cliff jump and a not-that-lazy river (entrance fee required), as well as free use of a giant pool and a splash playground for little kids, making beach days even more fun for vacationing families.

To make it all more affordable, families should keep an eye on Norwegian’s Free at Sea promotion, which sometimes includes free third and fourth guest fares. That means that kids sharing a room with two paying adults sail free. Fares for seven-night Caribbean cruises start at $399 per person.

Families can have a great time on almost any cruise line, hanging out by the pool, visiting exciting new destinations and simply spending time together. But if you’re looking for a ship that really caters to kids and their adult companions, you’ll want to book a vacation with one of these five best cruise lines for families.
